incident_examples.text: Line 3, second shift. The bead on door seal frames started looking skinny about twenty minutes into the run — not missing, just anemic. The robot never tripped a hard fault, just kept cycling. We only caught it when QC flagged patchy coverage on the B-pillar parts. Nothing dramatic, just slowly losing oomph on the delivery side over the course of about half an hour.

Line 1, midday. Robot was mid-seam on a door frame when the whole thing just died in about two seconds — one moment normal, next moment the gauge hit the peg at zero. Heard a thud from the pump cabinet right before it happened. Nothing gradual about it at all, totally different from when we've had drift problems.

Second shift on line 4. The robot was running through its dispensing path on a bumper bracket when everything cut out instantaneously. Checked the delivery gauge and it went from a completely normal reading to basically nothing in a single heartbeat. Way different from the slow-drift issue we had last month — this was a cliff.

Line 2, night shift. Robot tripped a fault and we heard a loud thump from the hose bundle near the pump. When I looked at the gauge it was pegged way above the normal max. We backed away from the hose area because the fitting near the pump outlet looked like it was under serious stress.

Chassis line dispenser, afternoon shift. The unit kicked a hard fault and stopped mid-path. Panel gauge was reading way above the operational ceiling. The operator mentioned the hose was visibly bulging at the bend coming off the pump outlet just before the fault tripped.

Line 3, morning shift. The robot is still running cycles but the bead looks stringy in spots — like it's fighting to push material through. Got a yellow warning on the panel, not a red stop. There's visible buildup on the track below the tip but the material is still coming out, just not at full volume.

Line 1 operator. Getting inconsistent coverage on the roof ditch seam — some sections fine, others starved. The gun arm is still moving and the robot isn't stopping itself, just seems like the tip's got something partially in the way. Material is coming out, just not enough of it in the thin spots.

Line 4 dispenser — robot's moving the arm through the full dispensing path but absolutely nothing is coming out the tip. Pump is running, I can hear it humming away, but zero material is reaching the part. It's like the end of the nozzle is completely sealed shut.

Second shift, line 2. Quality stopped the line because three panels in a row came through the dispensing station with zero adhesive on them. Robot was going through its normal motions otherwise. Complete dry fire — nothing coming out despite everything appearing to run.

Line 1 operator. The dispenser has been getting sluggish over the last few cycles and the sight glass on the tank looks almost empty — you can nearly see the bottom. Robot flagged something on the panel but hasn't shut down production yet. Someone needs to check the material level before we run out mid-cycle.

Night shift, chassis line. About a half hour before the tank ran dry the robot started pulling air into the feed line — you could actually see bubbles moving through the clear section of the tubing. Nobody had checked the material level since the beginning of the shift.

QA flagged a batch from line 3 — the seal lines look like threads, way too skinny for spec. Robot was running normal cycle times, no alarms, arm moving fine. But the adhesive traces on the parts are maybe half the width they should be. Nothing screaming from the machine itself.

Second shift quality check, roof seam station on line 2. The vision system started kicking rejects but the robot wasn't stopping itself. Pulled a few parts and the adhesive lines are definitely starved — thin traces barely covering the flange edge. Machine thinks everything is fine.

Line 4, door seal station, afternoon run. The adhesive is squishing out way past the flange on both sides of the seam. Parts coming down the line are a mess — glue everywhere. The seam line is easily twice the width it should be, maybe more.

Morning shift, line 1 B-pillar station. QC pulled several parts because the sealant bead was grossly oversized — looks like the tip wore out and now it's flooding the flange instead of laying a proper line. Camera flagged it but the robot kept going through its cycles.

Line 2 pump area. Small puddle of adhesive forming under the hose connection near the pump outlet — maybe a shot glass worth accumulated over the last hour or so. Not spraying, just slowly weeping from the fitting. Sticky mess on the floor but not an emergency situation.

Maintenance tech here. Came back from break and found a slow drip from the coupling joint under the dispenser arm on line 3. It's been collecting on the drip rail below — not a lot of material, but it's been going long enough to leave a sticky stripe across about two feet of floor tile.

Line 4 emergency — the big supply hose under the loading dock dispenser let go and adhesive is spraying everywhere. The floor around the whole unit is already covered. Robot tripped itself but there's a lot of material out there already. Need help over here right now.

Night shift, chassis line dispenser. Heard a loud pop and then the whole cabinet started dripping adhesive from every seam. The spread covered about ten feet of floor in under thirty seconds. We cleared the area and hit the wall button immediately.

Safety officer called in from line 2. Massive adhesive release — the feed line connection at the pump head came completely apart. There is a significant slip hazard covering the entire unit footprint. We've got personnel keeping others back while we wait for the response team.

Line 1 dispenser, second shift. The pump quit with a grinding noise and the breaker on the cabinet popped. Robot arm stopped mid-travel and the whole unit went into fault. Motor cabinet feels warm to the touch and the drive display is showing an error code I haven't seen before.

Maintenance tech on line 3. Motor on the adhesive pump stopped suddenly and the whole dispenser locked up. There's a fault indicator lit on the drive controller — the motor ran rough and erratic for a few seconds before it quit. Amperage indicator on the cabinet door gauge was pegged well above the normal band.

Quality engineer on line 2. The vision system stopped reporting bead data entirely and the monitor just shows a black screen. Robot is still running dispense cycles normally but we have zero visibility on whether the beads are in spec. Camera has completely gone dark.

Line 4, morning shift. The inspection display above the dispenser has been cycling through error frames for the last ten minutes — sometimes a frozen still image, sometimes just blank. Robot isn't stopping itself but QA can't sign off on parts without a live feed from that system.

Line 3 operator. We're at the four-hour mark and the tip of the gun is getting crusty around the edges — old adhesive building up where it didn't wipe clean from the last run. Not causing problems yet but it's past time for a clean cycle before it starts affecting the bead.

Second shift, door seal dispenser. Supervisor asked us to run a purge because the previous crew skipped their interval cleaning. There's visible residue on the nozzle face and the last few beads looked ragged at the start of each stroke — like the tip's not clearing itself properly.

Maintenance tech, line 1. We're at the service interval for the in-line strainer on the pump side. The differential pressure across the filter body has been creeping up on the last few logged readings — not quite at the limit but close. Time to swap the element before it starts restricting flow.

Maintenance call on line 4 dispenser. The gearbox on the pump drive is starting to sound a little dry — faint whine when it ramps up to speed. Checked the PM log and we're past the scheduled grease service interval.

Line 1, preventive maintenance. The lube reminder flag came up on the control log for the pump drive assembly. The tech who did the previous PM noted the fitting was already running a bit dry back then, so we want to get grease in there before it starts making noise.

Line 3, first shift. Supervisor authorized a material top-up because we're heading into a long production run and the tank is sitting around 15 percent. We've got a drum already staged at the machine and need to run the fill sequence to get back to capacity.

Loading dock dispenser. We already got the low-level flag earlier this shift and now we've got a fresh cartridge ready to go in. Supervisor signed off and the robot is sitting in hold mode waiting for us to get material back in the system before production can resume.

Quality engineer on line 2. Bead measurements from the vision system have been reading about half a millimeter narrower than what we actually measure on parts with a caliper. Something has drifted in the camera setup — the system and physical reality no longer agree.

Line 4, third shift QA check. The automated measurement system started flagging borderline rejects on parts that look perfectly fine visually. Compared camera output to a hand measurement and the numbers don't match by a noticeable margin — the system needs to be zeroed back to reality.

Maintenance supervisor on line 1. The feed hose on the main dispenser has a blister near the mid-section and the outer jacket is cracking at the bend radius. We've had two minor weeps from that same hose this month already — time to put a new one on before it turns into something bigger.

Line 3 dispenser. The hose is at or past its service life — pulled the log and it's over a thousand hours. The tech who last inspected it noted swelling at the pump end fitting. We're doing the changeout now rather than waiting for it to fail on us during production.

Maintenance tech on line 2. We've got a tech going into the pump cabinet to swap the pressure regulator. Before that door opens we need full energy isolation and tagging — there's stored pressure in that cabinet and the material is still at operating temperature.

Line 4. Safety coordinator flagged that the last nozzle changeout on the loading dock unit was done without proper isolation. We're redoing the full isolation procedure before the next job — tech needs physical access to the arm assembly and we are not cutting corners on this one.

Line 1 emergency — there's smoke coming from underneath the dispenser unit near the pump cabinet. We don't know if it's from the motor or the adhesive lines but there's a strong burning smell and we've already started moving people away from the area.

First shift, line 3. Coming in cold this morning — unit has been off all weekend for the holiday shutdown. Everything was locked out Friday afternoon so we're starting completely from scratch for the Monday production run.

Line 2, wrapping up day shift. Need to clear the gun and get the pump down before the cleaning crew comes in. Last time someone left without capping the nozzle we had material skin over the tip and it took twenty minutes to clear it before first shift could start the next morning.

Line 4, end of night shift. Production is done for the night and we need the dispenser shut down properly. The material in the hose has to be cleared out so it doesn't cure overnight and block the line for first shift tomorrow.

Running the number 2 dock on the east wall — the unit kept beeping at us all morning, third shift said the same thing. Checked the readout and it's sitting around 22 volts, which isn't enough to top off the big counterbalances but it didn't cut out either. Nobody wanted to kill the line over it but the yellow light on the panel has been on since 6 AM.

The AGV on lane 4 came back and sat at the dock for nearly 45 minutes before the battery even hit 60 percent. Normally it's topped up in 20. Power meter on the dock is reading low — just under nominal — but the unit is still running, just slow. No red alarm, just the amber warning.

Second shift noticed the charge dock by the stamping exit wasn't keeping the fleet topped up. It's supplying power but the gauge is showing something like 23 point something, which is technically on but not right. Panel light is amber, not red, and the AGVs are finishing their cycles way behind schedule.

Dock by bay 7 just died mid-charge. The AGV was sitting there and the whole thing went dark in about two seconds — voltage went from normal to basically nothing instantly. Had to pull the vehicle out by hand. This wasn't a brownout that faded in, it was a sudden drop.

Panel on the dock near the assembly cell was screaming — red light, continuous alarm beeping. Looked at the output gauge and the number was way up past where it should ever be. Shift lead was worried we were cooking the AGV battery packs.

Got a call from first shift that dock 1 was kicking out every vehicle — AGVs would seat and then immediately reverse out. Checked the screen and the output ceiling was blown past by a good margin. The dock was running hot electronically speaking.

The charge dock by conveyor 6 was humming louder than usual and tripped the breaker twice in one shift. Amp reading on the display was well over what's normal — the thing was pulling way too hard. AGV battery wasn't even fully depleted when it started, so it's not like the vehicle was starving for power.

AGV pulled into the dock on line 2 and the charge never started. Vehicle just sat there blinking. When we looked at the contacts, the pads were not lined up — visible gap on one side. The machine made mechanical contact but not a real electrical connection.

Had an AGV that kept throwing a no-charge fault right after docking. Vehicle was physically inside the pocket but something was off — the contact faces looked skewed when you got close and looked at them. The dock unit by the loading door has been doing this intermittently all week.

The AGV on rotation 4 was creeping into the dock like it was dying. Took almost three minutes to close the last foot of travel. It eventually made contact but it was painfully slow. No fault code on the vehicle display, it just was not moving at the right speed.

First shift said the unit in aisle C was crawling when it came back for a recharge. Still moving, but barely. A few guys thought the floor was wet but it did the same sluggish approach two runs in a row on a dry surface.

Dock 5 by the weld cell — the AGV approach has been sluggish all day. It is not stopping, it is just way slower than it should be going into the pocket. Takes roughly twice as long to dock as the other units on the same circuit. Still getting there, but the cycle time is way off.

AGV on route 2 rolled up to the dock, got about eight inches away from the contacts, and just stopped dead. Would not move another inch. No alarm on the vehicle itself, and it never made contact with the charging contacts. Had to push it in manually to get a charge started.

Line 4 dock — the vehicle pulled in, got close, and froze completely. Just sat there not moving at all. The dock sensors must have seen it coming but it never reached the contacts. Happened twice this morning on the same vehicle and the same dock.

Maintenance found an AGV parked in front of dock 3 but not connected. It was just stopped short, not touching anything. Driver said no errors came up on the panel. You could see the vehicle sitting right at the dock entrance but it had completely given up before making contact.

The detection gear on dock 2 near shipping was acting up — sometimes it would see the AGV coming in, sometimes it acted like nothing was there even with the vehicle sitting right in front of it. The dock would not initiate a charge because it thought the spot was empty.

The dock on the far end of the floor stopped recognizing AGV arrivals entirely. The vehicle would seat fine mechanically but the system thought the spot was vacant. The tech confirmed it is not the vehicle causing it — the detection eye on the dock side is reading nothing.

Flash and a bang from dock 6 during second shift — loud enough that two workers on the line flinched and stepped back. Smelled like burnt insulation right after. The AGV that was docked rolled backward on its own. Nobody hurt but we cleared the area immediately.

Line 1 charging station threw sparks during connection on first shift. One of the operators saw a bright flash at the contact point and heard a sharp pop. The system faulted itself out but not before the smell filled the corner of the bay. Real electrical event, not a tiny flicker.

The charging unit on the south side of the plant was hot to the touch on the housing — way hotter than normal during any previous shift. The internal fan sounded labored and strained. We checked and the temperature gauge was in the red zone but the unit was still trying to charge.

Saw a small flicker when the AGV connected at dock 3 during first shift — quick little spark, gone in half a second. The system did not alarm, no smell, and the charge started normally right after. We know to log anything like this even if it looks minor and the dock kept running.

Operator on line 2 said he saw a tiny blue flash when the vehicle seated into the dock contacts. Lasted maybe a tenth of a second and the dock kept running like nothing happened. No alarm lit up, no odor. He wanted it logged just to be safe. Everything looked fine afterward.

Maintenance pulled the pad inspection this morning on dock 4 and they are basically paper-thin. The wear indicator was in the red and the contact surfaces look burned and pitted all the way across. They cannot be cleaned back to usable, they need to come out entirely.

The pads on the charging contacts at station 2 are shot — we have been cleaning them every week but they are down to almost nothing. Resistance readings across the connection have been creeping up and a couple of recent charges were incomplete because the surface is too degraded to hold a good connection.

The guide rails on dock 1 are squealing every time an AGV comes in for a charge. Started last week and has been getting louder since. The vehicle also jostles noticeably on entry compared to the other docks which still slide in smooth. Nobody can find a record of these rails ever being lubricated since install.

There is a grinding noise from the dock slide on unit 5 near the paint line. Every time an AGV pulls in you can hear the rail resistance. The contact arm actuator also feels stiff when the tech manually operates it during a vehicle swap. Getting worse week over week.

The proximity sensor on dock 3 has been triggering too late — AGVs are almost fully seated before the system even acknowledges arrival. Used to register the vehicle at about a foot out. Now it barely fires until the vehicle is nearly touching. It has been about three months since anyone checked the calibration on that unit.

Dock 2 sensor was calling vehicles as present when they were still 18 inches away from the pocket, and then missing them when they were actually docked and making contact. The readings are just off across the board — not broken, just drifted. Probably needs a re-zero.

The cooling fan on dock unit 4 has been running at maximum speed all shift but the unit is still running warmer than normal. Checked the back filter and it is completely packed with lint and metal grinding dust. Barely any airflow getting through it at all.

Maintenance flagged dock 2 — the pressure drop alarm came on last week and nobody addressed it before the weekend. Filter looks like it has not been swapped in months, completely blocked. Unit is still running but it is overworking itself and the temp is climbing.

The contact pads on dock 3 have a grayish film on them — looks like oxidation or maybe fine machining dust from the nearby press. Charging is still working normally and no alarms are up, but the weekly wipe-down is due and a tech noticed it looks grimy. Pads still have plenty of material left.

One of the techs noticed a light coating of dust and a few small metal chips sitting on the contact faces at dock 1. Nothing alarming, just the normal accumulation from the shop floor environment. The pads are not worn, just dirty. Due for the regular scheduled cleaning.

Electrical tech needs to swap out the charge controller board on dock 5 — put in a request for a full lockout before anyone opens the cabinet. Standard isolation required before any hands-on work inside that unit. No emergency, just planned board replacement.

Maintenance has a bearing swap planned on the dock guide actuator on unit 3 this afternoon. They submitted the LOTO ticket at the start of shift. Need the unit fully de-energized and tagged before anyone gets their hands inside the mechanism.

Smoke was coming from the top of the charging unit on the north wall — thin wisps but definitely smoke. Shift lead yelled to clear the area and kill it. We needed everything off fast and could not wait around for any kind of normal sequence.

Coming back from the long weekend — first shift lead wanted to make sure the dock was reading correctly before letting any AGVs queue up for a charge. Did a full go/no-go check on all sensors before releasing vehicles to the charge lane.

We were returning from a 4-hour planned downtime for the floor wax crew. Dock 2 needed to be verified and authorized before going live again. Supervisor asked for a complete sensor and output check before the first vehicle was allowed to charge on that shift.

End of day Friday — last vehicle finished its charge and the shift lead wanted the dock unit properly powered down before the weekend. Normal procedure, just needs to be logged and signed off for the maintenance crew coming in Saturday.

Dock 3 was being handed over for a weekend maintenance window. Second shift finished the last charge cycle and needed to bring the unit down in a controlled sequence before the maintenance crew arrived Sunday morning. No issues, just the standard handover.

Monday morning, first thing — foreman asked for the standard go-through on all docks before trucks started their first routes of the week. Nothing specific wrong, just the routine start-of-day checklist before loading the first AGV onto the charge lane.

Supervisor wanted documentation on dock conditions before a scheduled customer plant audit this afternoon. Tech ran through all the standard checks at the start of day shift and logged everything so the records would be current for the walkthrough.

Bi-weekly check time for the contact pads on dock 4 — just measuring, no plans to pull them yet. Pads still look OK visually but we track the numbers every two weeks. Not at the swap threshold yet but maintenance wanted the wear trend documented.

Been watching the main panel gauge on line 3 all morning and the needle has been creeping south since about 6 AM. Was sitting at 92 when I clocked on, now it is down to 86 and the air tools are starting to feel sluggish. No alarm tripped, no banging, machine is still humming - just a slow bleed over the last couple hours.

Second shift here by the loading dock compressor - our air guns started feeling weak maybe an hour into the shift. Checked the big gauge on the panel and it is reading 84. Nothing has alarmed, the unit is still cycling, but we have been slowly losing ground since around 2 PM. No sudden anything, just a gradual drift downward.

Big pop from the compressor room - I was on the floor maybe 30 feet away and felt it in my chest. Ran over and the system gauge went from 105 to near zero in about 10 seconds flat. Compressor is still spinning but there is absolutely no air anywhere on the lines. Happened in an instant.

Every robot on line 2 faulted simultaneously - all the air grippers dropped parts at the same time. Ran to the compressor panel and we are reading 3 PSI. Was over 100 not 10 minutes ago. There was no slow drop, no warning - it just went away all at once.

Heard what sounded like a gunshot from the utility corridor on third shift. The plant overhead PA auto-announced a total air loss. By the time I got to the compressor area the needle was pegged at zero. One of the guys said it dropped off the scale in under 15 seconds. Never seen anything go that fast.

High-pressure alarm lit up on the HMI screen and the red beacon on the compressor cabinet is flashing. The panel gauge shows 128 PSI. The machine is fully loaded and just keeps pushing - the unload cycle never kicked in on its own. No shutdown, just the alarm light and a climbing gauge.

Doing my morning rounds and noticed the pressure gauge on the receiver tank is pegged higher than I have ever seen it - 132 PSI. The unit is running but the unload cycle has not fired once since I started watching. It is just sitting there overpressure with no automatic relief from the controls.

The amber light on the compressor cabinet came on but the machine did not shut down. Walked over and the digital readout on the panel shows 203 degrees. Felt the discharge pipe and it is noticeably hotter than usual. She is still running fine otherwise - no fault, just the yellow beacon going.

Was cutting through the compressor room on my way to the break room and noticed the amber warning light cycling on and off. Checked the panel temp display - sitting at 198. Machine is loaded, air is flowing, no shutdown. That yellow beacon has been flashing for at least 10 minutes based on when I walked by last time.

Compressor just shut itself completely off - went silent mid-shift. Red fault light is solid on the cabinet. Went to the panel and the temp readout shows 215. The machine tripped itself out automatically - no air, no running, nothing. Tried the start button once and it would not come back on.

Night maintenance called me in because we lost all air. The big unit on the east wall is stone cold dead - just sitting there with the red lamp on. Temp display on the front panel reads 213 and it shows an automatic shutdown event from about an hour ago. Pushed reset and nothing happened.

Can hear a little hiss coming from the back of the storage tank near the drain valve fitting. Checked the gauge and we are losing maybe a PSI or so every minute - compressor is cycling more often to keep up but nothing has alarmed yet. The leak is small, more of a whistle than a roar.

Loud bang like a rifle shot from the compressor room - ran in and there is a crack running along the side of the tank. Air is screaming out of it, gauge dropped to zero in maybe 20 seconds. Room sounds like a jet engine. Everybody out of there.

The storage vessel just let go - saw the safety panel on the side of the receiver blow completely off. Massive rush of air, the whole compressor room filled with mist instantly. Lost all plant air in about two seconds. Was over 100 PSI one moment and zero the next.

Was maybe 10 feet away when it happened. The bottom seam on the big tank separated - made a sound like a concussion grenade. Air blasting everywhere, tools dead plant-wide. Can see the gap in the tank seam from outside the room and the gauge has been at zero since it blew.

Oil low lamp came on the compressor panel about 20 minutes ago during my walk. Looked through the sight glass on the front of the unit and the level is well below the bottom mark. Machine is still running - pressure is fine, temp is fine - just that amber oil light is on.

Second shift startup and the amber oil indicator was already lit when I came in to turn things on. Checked the sight glass before I touched the start button - barely any oil showing. Temp looked okay, everything else was normal, but whoever ran last shift either did not check or ignored it.

Night maintenance flagged this one on the handoff sheet. The oil status light on the control cabinet has been on since about 10 PM. Sight glass is down near the very bottom of the visible range. Unit has been running all night with that indicator lit.

Hour meter on the compressor rolled past 2000 sometime last week. Service label on the cabinet says it is past due. Oil in the sight glass looks darker than it should and has a slightly burnt smell when I pulled the dipstick cap.

Lab results came back on the quarterly oil sample I pulled last week. Viscosity is out of spec and the iron particle count is higher than the allowed limit. Need to get it drained and refilled before the next production run.

The intake restriction indicator jumped past the red line on the filter gauge this morning. Unit is working noticeably harder to breathe - you can hear the difference in the inlet sound compared to normal.
Oily mist showing up in the air line at one of the downstream drops on line 2. Checked the separator gauge on the panel and it reads 12 PSI across the element. That is way past the change point.

Squealing from inside the compressor cabinet every time it loads up. Opened the belt cover to take a look and there is a crack running about 2 inches along the outer edge of the drive belt. Ready to go any time.

Maintenance calendar flagged the 1000-hour belt inspection this week. Pulled the guard and the belt is significantly glazed on the pulley-contact side - no squealing yet but the glazing means it has lost its grip. Would not make it to the next interval.

Dew point alarm went off on the dryer unit this morning. We are getting moisture in the air lines - had two air-actuated valves seize up on line 1 already. Checked the filter differential indicator inside the dryer cabinet and it is pinned in the red zone.

Hit the 1000-hour mark on the dryer service log and pulled the coalescing element for inspection. It is completely waterlogged and the indicator was maxed out. Should have been changed before this but it got pushed back twice.

Maintenance PM sheet shows we hit the 2000-hour grease interval on the motor and fan bearings last Tuesday. Have not had a chance to get to it yet. The motor side has been quieter than usual which actually worries me - probably running dry.

Noticed a slight hum from the fan end of the compressor during my afternoon rounds. Touched the bearing housing on the fan side and it is noticeably warmer than the motor end. Greasing interval is overdue by about 50 hours on the log.
Annual safety walkthrough is coming up next week and the PRV on the receiver has not been pull-tested yet this year. Tag on the valve says last test was 13 months ago - we are already overdue.

Compressor is kicking on at 82 PSI instead of the 88 it should cut in at, and it is cutting out at 122 instead of 110. The cycling is all wrong. Six-month calibration interval is due anyway so this is probably drift in the switch.

Need to get inside the compressor enclosure to replace the minimum pressure check valve - the seat is shot and it is leaking back. Tech cannot open that cabinet until the machine is fully de-energized and locked out. Nobody goes near the internals without the lock on the disconnect first.

Scheduled to swap the inlet unloader valve this afternoon. Work order says the tech needs to reach inside the pressurized enclosure. All energy has to be isolated and tagged before anybody touches it - this is not a quick outside-the-cabinet job.

Oil puddled on the floor under the compressor when I came in this morning - the drip pan overflowed overnight. Looks like at least a quart on the concrete near the east wall. Definite slip hazard and it is spreading toward the aisle.

Drip pan under the unit is overflowing and oil is running across the floor toward the storm drain. Happened at some point during second shift - floor is slick all the way to the equipment rack. Someone is going to go down if we do not get this contained.

Saw smoke coming out from the top vent slots of the compressor cabinet during third shift rounds. Strong smell like burning plastic or insulation. Nobody was in the room when it started - I noticed it from outside through the window.

Small flame visible at the back of the motor control panel inside the compressor room right after first shift startup. Wiring smell immediately. Looks like it started at one of the contactor terminals.

First shift is starting and we need to get the compressor online before assembly begins at 6. Shutdown last night was clean - no faults showing on the panel, no red lights, no LOTO in place. Just a normal morning bring-up.

End of third shift and production is done for the week. Management wants the compressor shut down for the weekend - no maintenance work orders active, just a clean stop and walk-away. Nobody needs access to the machine, just get it parked safely.

Monday morning and the maintenance coordinator wants the compressor inspection sheet filled out before the 9 AM production meeting. Last week flagged a couple of amber items to keep an eye on so need to walk through everything and log the current state.

Plant manager is asking for this week's compressor health log before the noon review. Need to go through all the checkpoints on the form, pull the readings off the panel, and get it signed off. Has not been done yet this week and it is already Wednesday.

Second shift, unit by the east wall — the output started feeling weak around 2 AM. Stamping line 4 kept stalling because the headers weren't giving enough oomph. Checked the gauges and the needle was sitting around 78 on the main header, just kind of drifted there over about 20 minutes.

Line 2 forming press started throwing fit warnings because the die wasn't seating right — traced it back to the boiler room. The burner had been running at half capacity all morning and nobody noticed the header reading had been creeping down since 6 AM. Nothing dramatic, just slowly losing ground.

Everything was fine then boom — the whole boiler room header went from 110 to 85 PSI in less than a minute. You could hear it on line 1, the forming units all stalled simultaneously. Maintenance thought a line had blown somewhere downstream.

Third shift, around 3 AM, the control room alarm lit up red all at once. Operator said the needle dropped like a rock — wasn't a slow thing at all. Took maybe 30 seconds to lose over 20 pounds. We shut the header valve immediately, couldn't figure out if it was a rupture or a valve failure.

Yellow caution light came on at the main panel around 10 AM. The gauge was reading 128 PSI — still under the pop-off but definitely over where we're supposed to run. Fired down to low and cracked the vent, got it back under control within a few minutes. Logged it and told the super.

Line 3 operator noticed the steam was hitting the molding press harder than usual and there was a yellow indicator on the panel. Went to check and the header was up at 131. Not dangerous yet but creeping higher than we want. Adjusted firing rate and watched it come back down into the green.

Morning startup on the big boiler near the compressor bay — gauge climbed higher than normal after warmup, sat around 127 PSI and the warning light was on. Relief hasn't popped, just a caution situation. Turned the burner down and vented a bit to bring it in range before the day shift came on.

Loud hissing from the roof vent near boiler 2 — first shift operator ran out and confirmed steam was shooting out the pop-off. The panel read over 150. Killed the burner immediately and shut the feedwater. Cleared everyone out and called the safety officer, nobody goes back in until it bleeds down.

Boiler near the stamping room started alarming around noon. Operator went to check and the sight glass showed barely any water — level was down low, not where it should be at all. Feedwater auto system wasn't keeping up. Hit the pump start and monitored until it came back up to safe range.

Second shift maintenance found the drum reading at about 25% on their hourly walk. It had been dropping for a while — the auto makeup wasn't filling fast enough because one of the float valves was gummed up. Started the pump manually and checked flow before calling the supervisor.

Tech on line 4 area noticed the boiler by the paint bay wasn't performing right — steam quality looked wet and sluggish. Checked the drum indicator and the level had gradually dropped below the red mark. Nothing sudden, just slowly depleted over a couple of hours without anyone catching it.

The drum went from half full to nearly empty in about 45 seconds — I've never seen it drop that fast in my four years here. We think the blowdown valve stuck open or a tube let go somewhere inside. Killed the fire instantly and tried to force feed. Safety officer got a call right away.

Line 2 forming presses were banging and popping — classic water hammer through the headers. Came back to the boiler room and the drum was way too full, up around 90%. The feedwater auto-fill must have stuck on. Stopped the pump and did a surface blowdown to pull the level back down.

Startup operator on first shift overfilled the drum — flooded the steam space. The header pipe on the south side was knocking and vibrating audibly. Went to the control panel and the level reading was sitting at 88%. Stopped the feedwater pump and opened the surface blowdown until we hit about 60%.

Boiler near dock 3 went into lockout around 6 AM — the burner tried twice and couldn't catch. Control box had the fault light on solid. Tech hit the reset button, waited about half a minute, and tried again. Second attempt it lit fine. Noted it in the log for the morning crew.

Middle of second shift the big boiler just went quiet — no combustion noise at all, no heat output. Operator checked and the igniter had failed to re-light after a normal cycling event and the safety system went to lockout. Had to get maintenance to reset it and re-fire before pressure got too low.

Stack thermometer by boiler 1 was reading 480 degrees when we did rounds at 8 AM — way hotter than normal exhaust. Maintenance figured the fire-side tubes were scaled up bad after months of high TDS water. Turned the firing rate way down and got someone to schedule a tube inspection.

Plant manager flagged that the stack on the north side boiler was putting out visible heat shimmer even at low load — neighbor complained about it. Instruments showed exhaust temps pushing 470 F. Throttled back the burner and called maintenance to schedule a fireside cleaning.

Primary feedwater pump on the east boiler just stopped mid-shift — tripped on overload. Drum level started trending down toward the caution mark. Kicked the backup pump on from the panel near the pump skid and kept an eye on the flow meter to make sure it was actually moving water into the drum.

Second shift operator said the drum wasn't climbing even with the pump supposedly running. Went to the pump room and the primary was humming but not actually pumping — impeller probably shot. Switched to the backup and confirmed flow on the meter before we left the area.

Small puddle forming near the bottom flange on boiler 2 — about a cup's worth of water over several hours. No alarms, all pressure gauges look normal. Put a drip pan under it and cracked the isolation valve closed. Told maintenance to get a new gasket on this one when they have a chance.

Cleaning crew noticed a slow wet spot on the floor in the boiler room corner early morning — traced it to a valve stem on the condensate return line. Just weeping slowly, not spraying. Nothing abnormal on the pressure gauges at all. We contained it with a pan and called the day-shift plumber.

Massive cloud of steam filled the back half of the boiler room right near shift change. One of the guys near line 4 saw the pipe elbow let go — water and steam just everywhere at once. Hit every shutoff we could reach and got everyone out immediately. Called safety, nobody re-enters until cleared.

Scale buildup in the boiler tubes looked worse than normal during inspection last Tuesday — traced it to the softener skipping its last cycle. The salt hopper was nearly empty too. Loaded two new salt bags and kicked off the regen manually. Told the supervisor it was done and logged the time.

Lab flagged elevated hardness on a feedwater sample they pulled — well above what we want going into the drum. Maintenance went to the treatment skid on the north side, checked the hopper level, added salt, and ran a full regeneration cycle. Water quality test passed when they checked again after the cycle finished.

TDS was reading around 3800 at the start of first shift — definitely time to purge the drum. Opened the bottom drain at the valve station for about 30 seconds, got the sludge moving good, then closed it back up. Checked the reading again and it had come back down into range. Logged it in the PM book.

Daily check showed it was past 72 hours since the last drain-off — got pushed because of the production crunch. Maintenance ran down to the valve, opened the bottom for a half minute, then closed it up. The water coming out was dark brown at first, almost black. Definitely needed doing.

Operator on first shift couldn't read the water level through the sight glass — there was a heavy brown film on the inside that made the scale impossible to see clearly. Locked it out at the LOTO board, cleaned it with the kit from the cabinet, and confirmed actual water level before signing off the shift.

Weekly PM was due on the level glass on boiler 1 per the maintenance calendar. It wasn't terrible but there was noticeable discoloration at the waterline and some mineral staining. Took the cleaning kit out, did the lockout procedure, wiped it down inside and out. Crystal clear afterwards — supervisor signed the PM log.

CO monitor near burner 2 started creeping up during steady firing — hit around 60 ppm which is above our threshold. Maintenance pulled the tip and it was noticeably eroded and pitted at the orifice. Grabbed the spare from the parts cabinet, swapped out the old one, and called maintenance to complete the reinstall and relight.

Hour counter on the main burner hit 2000 so we pulled the tip for scheduled swap-out. No obvious failure on it — just time-based per the manufacturer spec. Shut the burner down at the panel, accessed the burner head, pulled the old nozzle and staged the replacement, then notified the tech to finish the installation.

Monthly test day on boiler 3 — maintenance tech did the manual pop test while operating pressure was in the normal zone. It lifted cleanly and re-seated without any dribble or chatter. Checked the steam pressure gauge before and after to confirm it came back to normal. Signed off the PM card and told the supervisor.

During scheduled monthly checks on the north boiler, the safety valve lifted fine but was slow to reseat — sat slightly open for a few extra seconds longer than expected before clicking shut. Maintenance noted it for follow-up and informed the shift supervisor after checking that operating pressure had returned fully to normal.

Maintenance was coming in Saturday to reline the fireside of boiler 2 — needed full energy isolation before anyone could go inside the shell. Killed the burner, closed the main steam block valve, and locked everything out at the LOTO board. Handed over the keys to the maintenance lead for them to verify before entry.

Operator near the trap manifold on line 3 got hit with flash steam when a union fitting let go unexpectedly — second-degree burn on her forearm. Shut the main steam valve at the panel immediately, grabbed the first aid box from the station by the entry, and hit the emergency call button. Safety officer was on the phone within two minutes.

CO detector on the east wall of the boiler room started chirping and went to full alarm — reading was around 45 ppm. Figured it was the burner not getting enough combustion air. Killed the burner right away, hit the exhaust fans at the ventilation panel, got everyone out of the room, and called the safety officer to meet us outside.

Monday morning after a long holiday weekend shutdown — boiler near the north dock was completely cold and empty from the planned outage. First thing was checking if there was enough water in the drum before doing anything else, then getting the feedwater pump going to fill it up before we even thought about lighting the fire.

After the annual inspection, we had to bring the main boiler back from zero — it had been cold for four days. Filled the drum from empty, fired the pilot carefully, and let it build steam slowly. Kept checking the pressure gauge every few minutes until it reached normal operating range before calling the supervisor to confirm startup complete.

End of the production week Friday — scheduled to bring boiler 1 down for weekend maintenance access. Killed the burner at 3 PM, let the pressure bleed off naturally for about 10 minutes while watching the gauge, then closed the main steam header and stopped the feedwater pump before locking the room and leaving.

Plant manager ordered a controlled shutdown of boiler 2 for a Thursday afternoon inspection window. Second shift operator walked through the steps per the posted procedure — shut the fire first, waited for the gauge to show pressure coming down, then isolated the steam line and stopped the water pump. Supervisor confirmed all steps done before signing off.

First thing this morning on line 3, I hit the main switch and the torque head pressure gauge was sitting at zero. Waited a bit before punching cycle start — the machine had not stabilized yet. Radioed the super we were running late getting up.

End of third shift on line 2, I punched the stop and waited longer than usual before cutting main power — there were still a few bottles clearing the head. Checked the hopper light before I powered down and gave the super a heads-up we were clear.

Shutdown on the capper near the loading dock at end of day. Hit cycle stop and stood there watching it drain through. Made sure the hopper sensor read before cutting the main. Told the super everything was down.

Line 4, second shift around 1:30pm — the caps just stopped feeding mid-run out of nowhere. Looked in the chute window and they were all piled up in there, kind of bridged over each other. Had to kill the cycle and dig them out into the scrap bin.

The capper on the north side of the floor went silent about two hours in. No caps coming through the chute at all. I could see a solid wedge of plastic pieces wedged in there. Stopped the machine, cleared it, and got things running again.

Cap feed died on line 1 about an hour into the first run of the shift. Chute looked like a traffic jam — nothing was moving through it. Stopped the machine, pulled the stuck ones out and dropped them in the scrap bin, then brought it back up and checked the flow sensor.

Line 3 first shift — the alarm panel lit up red and I checked the torque readout, it was way past the upper limit. The head was really fighting those bottles hard. Happened on two cycles in a row, so I knew it was not a fluke. Stopped it and called maintenance to check the air.

The torque display on the capper near dock 2 kept pegging past the red line over and over. You could hear it straining on each cycle. Shut down and had maintenance look at the pressure to the head — something was too high in there.

Line 2, third shift — QC started flagging loose caps coming off the end of the line all the way through the run. I looked at the torque display and it was reading under the green band the whole time, not a spike, just consistently weak all shift. Stopped it, called QA and maintenance both.

QC on line 1 pulled three bottles in a row where the caps spun off easy with almost no force. I looked over at the gauge and it was sitting below the minimum on every single cycle. Not fluctuating at all — just stuck low the entire run.

The capper by the west wall had been running all morning but the numbers on the torque screen never climbed into spec even once. Caps were going on but they were not tight. QC inspector came over and confirmed they were consistently under-torqued across the whole batch.

Mid-run on line 3, the machine made a weird clunk sound and then the torque readout dropped to basically nothing in one shot. It was not gradual at all — one cycle it was fine, the next cycle the display showed zero. Hit the red button and got maintenance on it right away. Supervisor also came over.

The capper near the south end of the floor had been running all morning with no issues and then all of a sudden one bottle went through and the head just did not engage. The readout went flat in an instant — not low, just nothing. Had to e-stop it. Both maintenance and the supervisor showed up.

Line 4 — the vision system flagged a bad bottle but the reject arm never moved. Watched the bad bottle go right down the line. The gate position light on the panel was showing the wrong state. Stopped the machine immediately and radioed maintenance.

Second shift on the capper near dock 1, rejects were supposed to be kicked off the line but two just kept rolling past. Looked at the actuator status — arm never extended. Position indicator on the panel was stuck showing open when it clearly was not. Stopped it and called maintenance.

Noticed a crooked-capped bottle making it past the sort point without getting pulled. Watched it happen again before I stopped the line. The gate was not responding at all to the detection signal — position sensor on the panel confirmed it was showing the wrong mechanical state.

Line 2 around mid-morning, the yellow hopper light came on but the machine was still running fine and caps were still dropping normally. Had plenty of time, so I went over to the cap stock rack, grabbed a bag, and topped it off before it ever got to a stop situation.

The hopper warning light flickered on during first shift on the unit near bay 3. Caps were still flowing fine through the chute at that point. I went to storage, grabbed a full bag, and dumped it in. Never had to stop production or even slow down.

Line 3 just stopped capping out of nowhere — no caps hitting the head, machine just silent. Looked at the hopper and it was bone dry. Had to stop the cycle completely, go get a fresh bag from the cage in the back, dump it in, and restart from the panel.

The machine on line 1 quit feeding caps around 3pm. Red light on the hopper panel — not yellow, red. Nothing in the hopper whatsoever. Had to do a full cycle stop, restock the hopper from the supply area, then power the cycle back on from the main panel.

Weekly PM on line 4 today — maintenance calendar said it was grease day for the capper. Stopped the cycle, grabbed the grease cartridge from the maintenance cabinet, and worked it into the fittings on the torque head and drive chain. Called the tech to log it.

Hit the 500-hour mark on the operating counter for the capper near bay 2 during second shift. PM record said lubrication was due. Stopped the machine, pulled the grease from the cabinet, and got it into the torque head assembly. Notified maintenance to sign off on the PM card.

Weekly walk-down on line 3 Monday morning — the main drive belt had a visible crack running straight across it and it felt stretched and loose when I pressed on it. Pulled it off, dropped the old one in the scrap bin, and put the new one from the parts shelf on.

The capper by the north dock had a drive belt that was visibly fraying at one edge during my Monday inspection. Measured elongation against the reference mark and it was past the line. Stopped production and swapped it out for the spare we keep in the drive compartment.

QC flagged that the torque numbers on line 2 had been drifting around 8 percent over the last couple of days — bottles were coming off with noticeably different pull-off force bottle to bottle. Stopped the machine, ran calibration with the reference kit from the tool cabinet, then had quality sign off.

Someone on line 4 hit the red mushroom button — a glove got way too close to the torque head during a bottle change. Machine stopped dead mid-cycle. Radioed the supervisor, checked the area was clear, gave it 15 seconds, then released the button. Let the super know both when it stopped and when we were back.

Maintenance needed to get inside the capper near bay 4 to replace an internal worn part. Stopped the cycle, cut main power at the panel, walked over to the lockout board, pulled the hasp set, and applied it to the main disconnect. Called the tech to come in and do the work.

Planned service on the line 3 capper was on the schedule for Tuesday afternoon. Maintenance needed access to the inside. Did the full de-energize sequence — stopped the cycle, hit main power off, walked to the lockout station, applied the lock to the main disconnect, and notified the tech they were clear to open it up.

End of shift cleaning on line 2 — there was a grey dust buildup inside the chute and a couple of stuck plastic chips from damaged caps coating the walls. Stopped the machine, grabbed the brush from the cleaning supply cabinet, and ran it through the interior. Everything flowing clean after.

The reject lane camera on line 1 started showing a yellow indicator on the panel — not a full fault, just degraded signal. Nothing had slipped through yet as far as we could tell. Called maintenance to come look at the alignment and read the sensor a few times at both the panel and at the station to confirm it was drifting.

Line 3 mid-morning — bottles were still feeding but there were bigger and bigger gaps between them, noticeably slower than normal. Speed indicator was under the green zone on the panel but clearly still moving. Hit the speed-up button, waited, and checked again. Called maintenance when it did not fully recover.

The infeed belt on the capper near bay 1 was dragging along slowly — not stopped, just sluggish. You could tell by the widening gaps between each bottle coming in. Bumped the speed up from the panel control and monitored for a bit. Ended up getting maintenance involved since it kept creeping slow.

Line 4 second shift — bottles just stopped coming to the capper entirely. Belt was completely dead, not slow at all. The motor overload indicator was lit on the panel. Stopped the capper, read both sensors to confirm, and had maintenance do the motor reset.

First shift line 2, infeed conveyor just froze up completely — not gradual, it quit instantly. Motor fault light came on at the same moment. Stopped the capper cycle first thing, then waited for maintenance to come clear the overload and hit the reset on the motor drive.

Line 3 first shift — the amber fault lamp on the drive section of the panel lit up and the capper slowed down and quit. Pulled up the fault code on the display at the panel — definitely a drive fault code, not anything related to the motor overload. Called maintenance and flagged the supervisor.

Second shift on line 1, the drive fault indicator came on and the entire capper unit stopped. Read the code at the main control panel, then walked to the electrical box and read the display in there too. Had both maintenance and the supervisor over before anything was reset.

QC started pulling bottles with upside-down caps on line 2 this afternoon — several in a row. The machine was still running and the orientation indicator on the panel was clearly flagging something wrong. Stopped the cycle, opened the chute panel, and called quality before restarting.

Line 4 had a run of bad caps going on — tilted at a weird angle when they hit the torque head, you could see it. The orientation sensor panel flag was active. Stopped the cycle, opened up the chute access to inspect, got QA involved, and brought the line back up after checking the sensor read was clean.

Line 3 around noon — someone spotted grease on the floor right under the capper near the lubrication fitting on the side of the machine. Flagged the shift supervisor right away, stopped the capper, grabbed the absorbent pads from the red spill cabinet, laid them down over the slick, and let the super know when it was contained.

Second shift near the capper by the south exit, someone almost slipped on a wet patch spreading from under the machine base — looked like hydraulic fluid or gear oil. Radioed the supervisor before anything else, stopped production, grabbed the spill kit from the station by the pillar, and put the absorbent down over the whole area.

The capper on line 4 hit the 1,000-hour mark on the PM log this week. Stopped the cycle, walked to the filter station, pulled the old filter out — it was noticeably dark brown and clogged-looking — dropped it in the scrap bin, and put the new replacement in from the parts shelf.

The air supply pressure gauge on the torque head side of the capper near bay 3 was reading higher differential than normal this morning — the needle was past the red hash mark on the filter gauge. Stopped the machine, swapped the filter out for the replacement we had in supply, and disposal into scrap.

Line 3 case packer was running slow and sticky this morning. Boxes coming off with weak flap seals - they were peeling open by the time they hit the staging area. Checked the glue head and the adhesive looked thick and stringy, not flowing right. Display was reading noticeably under where we normally run temperature-wise.

The east-side case packer threw a yellow alarm on the glue system around 10am. There was a faint smoke haze coming off the nozzle area and the glue was real watery, running past the flap joints and dripping on the conveyor frame. Boxes had glue squeeze-out all over the outside.

Third shift on line 2 - glue was scorching bad. Could smell something burning from across the floor. HMI had a flashing alert and what was coming out of the nozzle was so thin it just ran right off the carton flap instead of bonding.

We were mid-run on line 1, maybe 400 cases in, and glue suddenly stopped sticking at all. Looked at the readout and the temp had dropped like a rock in under a minute - nothing gradual about it, just crashed from normal to way below usable in one shot. Completely different from when it just drifts low over a few hours.

Saw a yellow beacon on the packer dashboard around 2pm on line 4. Machine was still running fine, no slowdown or bad seals - just that advance flag telling us the tank was getting low. Had plenty of time to deal with it before it became a real problem.

End of line 3 packer flagged a yellow indicator during the morning run. No alarm, no stoppage - just the pre-warn light. Output quality was still fine. Shift lead asked us to check the level and top it off if we could get to it.

Line 2 packer went dead stop around 3pm shift change. No glue coming out at all - boxes were just going through with open flaps. Red alarm was screaming and the tank was completely bone dry. Full stoppage, had to hold the line.

Lost a good 12 minutes on line 5 because the hot melt ran out during peak hours with no advance warning being caught. Cases started coming off with unsealed bottoms and then the machine killed itself on the red alarm. Whole downstream area backed up.

Had a blank fold up accordion-style right at the mouth of the packer on line 3. Machine stopped and the infeed sensor lit. The blank had gotten creased bad by the feed rollers and wouldn't release on its own. Had to pull it out manually.

Packed boxes started backing up at the exit end of the line 4 packer. A finished case had rotated on the belt somehow - got crossways right after the tuck-flap station and blocked the next three coming out behind it. Machine kept trying to push more into the jam.

The loading arm on line 3 case packer seized up mid-cycle and threw a drive fault. Machine went into alarm and the whole unit stopped. Couldn't clear it with a normal reset - had to get maintenance involved to check if something was mechanically bound up inside.

Box blanks were coming through at a slight angle on line 4 during the afternoon run - about every fifth case had a misfolded bottom tab. Looked at the former and the belt was drifting to one side but still moving. No full stop, just inconsistent output.

Line 3 packer went completely dark on box erecting. The former belt had snapped and wrapped around the back pulley. No cases being formed at all - machine was cycling but nothing was coming out the erector.

Heard a loud snap from the packer near the press room right at the start of changeover. Found the former belt completely off - not slipping, not misaligned, just physically broken. Machine was trying to form cases on nothing and faulted out.

Conveyor on the case packer at line 6 started stuttering and then died outright mid-shift. Checked the control panel and there was a drive error code flashing. No jams anywhere on the belt - the belt itself looked completely fine, motor just wouldn't turn.

Line 1 packer conveyor stopped with no warning during the afternoon run. Panel was showing a drive fault code - not a jam, not a belt issue. Electrician said it was a drive trip, probably a thermal event in the cabinet.

Noticed a drip coming from behind the nozzle head on line 3 packer during my rounds. Slow but steady - had maybe a golf ball size puddle on the deck plate after about an hour of running. Boxes were still sealing fine, just made a mess on the frame.

Glue was seeping from a fitting near the nozzle manifold on the unit by dock 2. Not spraying or blowing out - just slowly weeping. Output quality looked OK but it was building up on the frame and dripping to the floor. Enough that someone could slip on it.

Hot melt hose on line 5 packer blew apart at the elbow fitting during first shift. Glue was spraying in a fan pattern - hit the floor, a nearby cable tray, and the side of the conveyor frame. Burns hazard, cleared the area immediately.

Second shift heard a pop from behind the glue unit on line 4 and then saw adhesive shooting out in a stream. An operator caught a splash on their forearm - minor burn, went straight to first aid. Full emergency shutdown, plant safety called in.

QC flagged inconsistent glue bead on line 2 output during their morning walk. Pulled the nozzle cover and found a carbon buildup around the orifice from dried adhesive that had charred. PM was due anyway - bead pattern was definitely affected.
PM check on line 4 packer - nozzle tip had a partial blockage of charred glue residue. Output was still running but the bead was narrower than spec on one side. Cleaning was on the weekly schedule.
Line 3 conveyor chain was squeaking badly during the morning run - could hear it from 10 feet away. Checked the PM log and lubrication was 2 days overdue. No faults yet but it was getting loud.
The transfer chain on the case packer at station 5 was getting noticeably noisy during the afternoon. Running rough and jerky on the return side. PM schedule showed we were past the grease interval.

Former belt on line 1 packer was showing cracks along the edge during the PM inspection on Saturday. Reached the scheduled replacement interval and the surface had visible wear grooves. Proactive swap before it fails in production.
Belt on the box erector at line 6 had visible splits and fraying at the splice seam during our monthly check. PM mileage showed it was at change-out time. Swapped it before the morning shift started.

Glue pressure was reading low on line 3 even though the tank was full. Maintenance figured it was a clogged filter and pulled the element - it was completely packed with char. Filter PM had slipped past due by about a week.
Running the morning pre-shift fill on line 2 packer. Tank was at about 30 percent - not in alarm, just the routine top-off before the day shift kicked in so we have a full buffer going into the run.

Ops supervisor asked us to top off the glue on line 4 before second shift took over. Still had around 40 percent in there but policy is to not hand off to second shift with less than half a tank. No alarms, just scheduled housekeeping.

Case packer on line 3 was misjudging the position of blanks after we swapped out the infeed section bearings yesterday. Cases were phasing wrong and missing the tuck every few cycles. Position reads were off from where the blank actually was.

After the maintenance rebuild on the erector drive over the weekend, line 1 packer was off on its timing coming into the former. Position sensor reads did not match actual case location. Had about a half-inch of drift from where it expected things to be.

QC walk on line 2 first thing in the morning - pulled 3 cases from the discharge end for sampling. One had a weak bond on the minor bottom flap, not fully adhered. Sent the last 20-minute production batch back for 100 percent review.

Shift supervisor called for a spot check on line 5 packer output after a customer feedback flag came in. Pulled 2 samples and found the end-fold overlap was about 3mm short of spec. Had to adjust the former and pull more samples.

Maintenance needed to go in and pull the former belt on line 3 packer. Before anyone went inside the guarded area, we had to fully de-energize and lock out the machine. Took about 10 minutes to get all the LOTO hardware in place.

Scheduled major PM on the line 6 case packer over the weekend. Both electrical and mechanical energy sources had to be isolated and locked out before the team would enter. Whole crew had personal locks on before anybody touched anything inside.

Operator on line 4 smelled something burning near the drive cabinet of the case packer around 9am. Hit the big red mushroom and cleared everyone from the area. Maintenance found a wire had shorted against the cabinet frame - would have been a fire if we hadn't stopped it.

Been watching the readout on the unit over by bay 4 all morning and the number on the suction gauge has been slowly creeping down since first shift started around 6. It's sitting around 38 now and hasn't bounced back. Yellow light came on about an hour ago but the compressor is still humming along, nothing dramatic, just drifting.

The panel on the chiller near the loading dock has had that yellow indicator lit since halfway through second shift. Asked Jimmy to check it and he says the gauge on the low side has been losing ground all afternoon — nothing sudden, just slowly going in the wrong direction. Unit is still running but the number won't come back up on its own.

I was standing right next to the unit by bay 4 and watched the suction pressure reading drop from about 62 PSI to basically single digits in under a minute. Nothing gradual about it — it just crashed. Heard a short hiss and then both gauges just tanked at the same time. Never seen it move that fast in ten years on this line.

Second shift on the press line — one second everything looked normal on the chiller panel, next second both pressure gauges fell through the floor. The whole event was maybe 45 seconds from normal to zero. Production already shut itself down through the interlock. Sounds like something let go somewhere in the loop.

Big red fault on the chiller panel over by line 3. The discharge gauge is reading way up in the 400s and the compressor sounds like it's straining hard. Noticed before this happened that one of the condenser fans out back didn't look like it was spinning at normal speed. Could be related.

High pressure fault showing red on the unit near the stamping area. Discharge side is reading way above where it normally sits during a regular run. Compressor ended up tripping itself out. It's been running warm in that section today so ambient might be a factor on top of whatever else is going on.

The chiller HMI on line 2 has a yellow warning showing. Process coolant coming out of the unit is reading a few degrees warmer than it should be, but parts are still making spec — just barely. Nobody hit any e-stops and the unit is still running. It's been sitting yellow for close to an hour now without clearing itself.

Hard shutdown hit all the tooling on line 1 mid-cycle. Traced it back to the chiller — full red alarm on the panel and the interlock killed the line. Went to feel the outlet pipe and it's running warm enough to be uncomfortable to touch, which is way off from normal. Every red indicator on the panel is lit.

Everything on line 1 went down at once mid-cycle during second shift. The chiller panel is showing all red and the interlock relay tripped the downstream equipment off. Outlet temperature on the display is way above anything we'd call acceptable even on a bad day. No warning led up to this, it just went straight to a full stop.

Something strange going on with the chiller for line 3 — coolant is coming out way too cold. One of the aluminum tooling manifolds actually had condensation freezing on the outside surface during second shift, which never happens. Think the control valve might be stuck wide open.

Flow feels sluggish on the unit serving the assembly area coolant loop. The readout is showing something but it's well below where it normally runs — maybe 70 percent of what it should be. Everything is still circulating, not stopped, but the inlet pressure at the pump looked low when I checked it manually. Unit hasn't alarmed yet.

Line 4 chiller pump seems like it's struggling today. The flow numbers on the panel have been running about 25 percent below normal since the start of second shift but it hasn't gone to zero. Wondering if the strainer basket is starting to plug up again — it was due for a cleanout a few weeks ago.

Coolant pump on the chiller unit near bay 2 just stopped dead. The flow sensor went to zero and it's been sitting there. Not reduced, not low — nothing is moving. Compressor is probably not happy running with no flow. Motor might have overloaded. Need someone to check the motor cabinet before we try to do anything.

One of the condenser fans on the chiller out back near the east exit is completely dead. Walked past during a break and the blade was sitting still while the other fan next to it was spinning normally. That's probably why the panel is showing a fault. Motor must have overloaded in that fan cabinet.

Electrical fault code on the chiller panel for the condenser section, not the compressor, not the pump — specifically the condenser. Went outside to the unit and confirmed the fan is not moving at all. Overload relay in the electrical box for that fan circuit is almost certainly what kicked out.

Chiller shut itself down on a fault during the afternoon shift and it's the compressor that's the problem, not the pump or the fans — those are fine. Went to check and the overload indicator on the compressor contactor is showing tripped. Discharge was running high before it went. Going to need a tech to review before we reset anything.

Whole chiller shut down, compressor faulted. Checked the fan — fine. Checked the pump — fine. The compressor motor overload relay is what tripped and it's sitting in a faulted state in the electrical cabinet. We want to know why it happened before anyone just resets it and restarts the machine.

Maintenance log shows we're past the 500-hour mark on the coolant filter on the bay 3 chiller. Going to swap it out during the next window. Filter housing is in good shape, just the element itself is due based on hours.

The differential pressure reading across the filter housing on the chiller serving line 5 is getting up there — it's ticking above where we normally change them out. We've got replacement elements in the parts room on the shelf. Scheduling the swap for this weekend's maintenance window.

Condenser coils on the chiller out behind the east wall look like they haven't been touched in months. The aluminum fins are visibly packed with dust, cottonwood, and some kind of debris from the parking lot. The approach temperature spread has been creeping up and this is almost certainly why.

Chiller efficiency has been dropping on the unit by the shipping dock and when I physically looked at the condenser coil section, the fins are dirty enough that you can barely see through them. Temperature split between ambient and leaving condenser is way off from our baseline. Coil cleaning is overdue.

Pump on the line 4 chiller has been making a faint high-pitched sound during first shift for the past couple days. Held my hand near the bearing housing and it felt noticeably warm. Hasn't gotten louder yet but it's early. Probably needs the grease fitting attended to.

PM schedule shows the bearing lubrication on the coolant pump for unit 2 is overdue by about two weeks — got pushed back when we had the weekend downtime canceled. Going to get in there with the grease gun during the next available break window before it becomes a problem.

Did the weekly walkaround on the chiller bank and the sight glass on unit 2 near the north wall is showing bubbles, which isn't how it normally looks. Might be low on charge or there's something in the loop. The room gas detector hasn't gone into alarm, just a low advisory, but the sight glass alone is worth looking into.

Faint chemical smell in the chiller room near the unit by bay 5 during the routine weekly walkthrough. Nothing strong, more like a background odor. Sight glass looked a little different — bubblier — compared to what it normally shows. Want someone to confirm there's no minor leak before we sign off on the week.

Weekly inspection on the chiller bank — the unit on the north wall has a sight glass that went from clear last week to showing some bubbling this week. Suction pressure also looks a little on the low end compared to normal for this time of year. Going to have maintenance check the charge and do a proper leak scan on that unit.

Did a spot check with a handheld thermometer during the morning walkdown on the line 2 chiller and the panel temperature display is off by almost two degrees from what the reference is showing. That's outside the tolerance we accept. Sensor probably needs to be recalibrated or replaced.

Drive belt on the pump for the unit over by bay 6 has some visible cracking along the inner surface — you can see the cracking if you flex it by hand. It also squeaks a little when you're standing close to the pump during startup. Probably a week or two from snapping on its own. Getting it scheduled.

Belt inspection on the line 3 chiller pump — there's about 6mm of slack when I push on the middle of the belt, which is past what we allow. Inner surface is also showing glazing. This one isn't cracked yet but it's not far off. Going to swap it out at the next planned window rather than wait for it to fail.

Flow started dropping on the chiller for line 1 this morning and when I put my gauge across the Y-strainer it's reading 10 PSI differential, which is well above the 8 PSI trigger. That basket is definitely plugged. Didn't change the filter recently so the restriction is at the strainer, not upstream of it.

Second shift reported intermittent flow dips on the line 1 chiller that would clear up for a bit then come back. Classic plugged strainer behavior. Checked the dP across the basket and it's reading high. Changed the coolant filter last month so that's not the culprit — it's the strainer basket that needs to come out and get cleaned.

We're going in to replace the pump mechanical seal on the chiller by dock 3 this weekend. Crew is staged and ready but need the full isolation done first — electrical disconnect, compressor, pump, the works — before anybody puts hands on it.

Scheduled condenser coil cleaning on the east wall chiller unit during Saturday's plant shutdown. Maintenance crew has the brushes and chemicals ready to go but we need to complete the energy isolation procedure before anyone gets up on that unit. No work starts until the hasp is on.

There's frost forming on one of the fittings at the back of the chiller unit near bay 2. Not a little bit of condensation — actual ice buildup on the outside of the joint. There's also a strong chemical smell in that corner of the room and the wall-mounted gas detector lit up the high alarm about ten minutes ago. We need to clear the area.

Third shift reported a sharp smell in the chiller room near the north unit. Came in to check and there's ice forming around a joint on the refrigerant line — you can see the frost spreading from the fitting. The room concentration sensor is reading elevated and it's been trending up, not down. Something is actively leaking.

Active refrigerant release at the chiller near the loading dock. Ice is growing on the outside of a pipe fitting on the high side line. The room detector went to high alarm about 10 minutes ago and the smell is strong enough to clear people out of that bay. Not a small seep — this is a real leak that needs the emergency response.

Three loud banging impacts came from the chiller next to press line 2 during second shift — three heavy knocks spaced about a second apart then the pitch changed. Operator called it in right away. No smoke yet and no smell but that mechanical noise was absolutely not normal and we're not going to wait around.

Small amount of smoke coming from the upper panel section of the chiller unit near line 4. Barely visible but definitely smoke, not steam. Electrical smell in the area. Nobody is waiting to see if it gets worse — unit needs to come down right now.

Maintenance just wrapped up replacing the pump seal on the unit by bay 3 and they've signed off the work order. Ready to bring it back into service. Pump and compressor have both been sitting cold with the power off for about 18 hours so we need to go through the startup sequence properly before we hand it back to production.

Production is going down for the long holiday weekend and the chiller bank on the south side needs to come offline tonight. Need to make sure the compressor goes first and we give it enough time before killing the pump — don't want to do it wrong and come back to a compressor problem Monday.

End of week Friday, last shift is done and we're powering down the line 2 chiller for a weekend cleaning and inspection. Need to follow the book on the sequence — compressor off first, pump stays on to let it equalize, then pump off — so we're ready to restart clean on Monday morning without any surprises.
Came in first thing on first shift and the CMM is completely dark — whole panel is dead. Tried moving the axes and got nothing. Realized nobody did the full boot-up before leaving last night.
Night crew confirmed they killed everything hard at end of shift. Machine is cold, controller is off, no air audible. Need to go through the whole wake-up routine before we can touch any parts.
End of second shift and the probe is still seated on the last part — nobody put it back in the holder before they walked off. Controller box is still live and humming.

Shift changeover and the previous operator just left the machine sitting there running — stylus hanging over the table, controller powered up. Need to park it properly and power down the box before third shift takes over.

Machine just came on but the thermometer on the wall shows 18 degrees in here. HVAC hasn't caught up yet after the weekend. Can't touch any inspection parts until the room gets to where it needs to be.

Got here first thing and the measurement room is at 17.5. Looks like the building heat was set back over the long weekend. We're going to be sitting here waiting a while before we're allowed to run any dimensions.
Over the last hour the air gage has been slowly creeping down — sitting around 5.0 bar now and the yellow light just came on. Nothing sudden, just a gradual slide downward.
The whole machine just slammed off — pressure went from about 6 bar to under 2 bar in maybe five seconds and the axes dropped. Sounded like something burst in the line.
