Start of first shift, line 4 — ran through all the pre-run checks before giving it the green light. Had to confirm the head was at temperature and the air was holding steady before calling the supervisor to approve the run.

Monday morning on the north labeler — machine had been cold and sitting all weekend. Went through the full checklist to confirm head temp was up, pressure was stable, and stock levels were good before we kicked it off.
End of second shift, line 3 — ran through the shutdown sequence after the last batch, let the head cool for a minute, then gave it a quick wipe so third shift would be starting with a clean head.

Start of the day shift, line 2 — new batch of parts meant we had to pull a sample label and run it through the scanner to confirm the barcode was good before ramping up to full speed. QC needed sign-off.

Been running line 4 since 7am and about an hour in the machine started throwing that low-gas alarm. Checked the readout on the panel — it was sitting at like 6.5 bar, been slowly creeping down since we loaded the last set of brackets. Didn't drop off fast, just drifted. Called it in to maintenance.

Was mid-cut on line 3 doing the door panel blanks and the gas just dropped. Like, instantly. One second it was fine, then alarm screaming and the sensor said 1.2 bar. Heard a hiss from somewhere behind the machine. Hit the big red button right away, then got safety on the phone.

Near the end of third shift on the unit by the south wall, the assist gas went to basically nothing mid-cycle. Didn't taper off, just fell off a cliff. Readout showed sub-2-bar in under two seconds, and there was a distinct smell of nitrogen in the area. Stopped everything and got safety involved immediately.

Line 1, cutting aluminum blanks. Suddenly the cut stopped, big alarm, gas pressure at the panel showing 0.8 bar — basically zero. Regulator on the cylinder bank looked like it was venting. This wasn't a slow drop, it was an instant crash. Full stop, called maintenance and safety both.

High-pressure alarm went off on the unit by line 6 during the stainless job. Checked the readout — showing 17.5 bar, well above where it should be. Machine automatically paused the program but we weren't sure what to do from there. Nothing hissing or leaking, just the alarm going. Reported to maintenance.

First shift, the machine on line 2 started alarming and the panel showed the gas pressure had climbed above the red line — 16-point-something bar. Nothing leaking, no hissing, but the machine halted itself. Tech came over and vented it back down before we resumed.

The chiller on line 5 was reading 23 degrees this afternoon, which is above where it normally sits during a run. Machine was still cutting fine, no red alarms, just that amber warning light on the chiller. Hot day in the plant, might be ambient. Reported but didn't stop cutting.

Mid-afternoon on second shift, the coolant temp gauge on the unit near the inspection staging area was creeping up — got to about 24 degrees. Everything still running, no emergency alarms, just the amber indicator lit up. We got maintenance to take a look and boost the fan.

Had to kill the laser on line 2 — the chiller temp hit 29 degrees and the red alarm was going off, not the amber one. That's the one that means the module could get fried. Stopped the cut immediately, whole job had to wait. Maintenance said the chiller pump was struggling badly.

Third shift, unit by the north exit. Temperature on the chiller climbed past 28 and kept going — got to 30 before we cut power to the laser head. The red fault light was flashing, not the amber warning. Everything shut down, called maintenance and the shift supervisor. Couldn't touch it until it cooled down.

We were running the thick mild-steel job on line 4 when the chiller went critical. Sensor reading 29.5 degrees — way past the caution level, that's the stop-everything threshold. Hit the E-stop, disabled emission. Supervisor said this was potential module damage territory, whole line was down for two hours.

Came in for first shift on line 3 and the chiller had its low-level light on. Opened the reservoir to check — yeah, it was below the MIN mark. Temp was fine, pressure fine, just low on fluid. Grabbed the jug from the storage cabinet and topped it up before the shift started.

Low coolant alarm on the unit near loading dock 2. Temperature was totally normal, it wasn't a heat issue at all — just the level sensor reading low. Maintenance came over and refilled it from the cabinet. Wasn't on the PM schedule for another two weeks but it was clearly low.

The machine on line 4 banged the nozzle into the sheet mid-program — must've been a curl on the blank from the coil. Heard the thud and it threw a fault right away. We hit E-stop, the collision sensor had tripped. Told the tech there was contact, job is on hold until they clear it.

Cuts were looking rough on line 6 — dross getting worse on the mild steel, edges not clean but still cutting through. Looked at the power readout and it was sitting around 87% of what the program calls for. Machine was still running, just not at spec. Paused the job and called maintenance.

Running thin aluminum blanks on line 5 and they were almost separating but not quite — parts hanging on by a thread. Checked the readings and the laser output was low, like 91%, right on the boundary. No fault codes anywhere, no error on the screen. Paused and called it in.

Line 2, middle of a production run. Laser just stopped firing — no arc, no beam, nothing coming out. Screen showing fault code F-04, emission indicator went dark. Not a power level thing, the source itself threw an error code. Hit E-stop, called maintenance, they're looking at the module.

Third shift near the end of the run, machine suddenly stopped cutting and threw a source error on the panel. Readout showed full-on fault, no emission whatsoever — totally different from the power-a-bit-low warning we sometimes see. That one still cuts. This was the machine completely refusing to fire at all.

Fume extraction on line 3 started alarming mid-shift. You could actually smell something faintly in the area — shouldn't smell anything when the extraction is working right. The airflow indicator on the panel was below the normal band. Paused the cut and called the tech.

Maintenance ticket came through for line 4's laser head — lens swap was overdue per the PM schedule. Tech came out, powered down emission, and did the lens change during the morning break. We were back up and running in about 20 minutes. No quality issues, just routine.

Quality caught a few parts off line 5 with inconsistent cut edges — not bad enough to scrap but definitely flagging. Maintenance said it was time for a nozzle check anyway. They paused the machine, pulled the nozzle, and found some spatter buildup around the tip. Cleaned it up.

During the shift changeover walkdown on line 3, the tech noticed the cover glass inside the cutting head was fogged up with haze — not the lens itself, just the protective window in front of it. Scheduled swap happened right there. Emission was disabled, old glass out, new one in. Different job from a full lens change.

Line 6 PM checklist said the cover window was due for replacement. Tech came during the lunch break, popped the head open, and the glass had oil haze contamination around the edges. Replaced just the cover glass, put the head back in service, and logged it. Lens itself was fine.

Monthly PM run on line 2's chiller. No alarm, no fault light, machine was running perfectly normal. Calendar said it was time to top off the coolant. Tech checked the level — about 80%, not low enough to trip any sensor. Topped it off from the storage cabinet as scheduled.

Maintenance came through line 4 for the routine coolant service on Tuesday. Chiller running fine, no warnings at all. Level check showed it was slightly down from last month, around 85%, topped it off as per the PM plan. Not the same as when the alarm goes off — this was just the planned monthly top-up.

The differential pressure on the exhaust housing for line 5 finally hit the saturation limit after a heavy month of stainless cutting. Tech swapped the filter during the lunch break. System was paused for maybe 15 minutes. After the change the airflow went right back up to normal range.

PM interval was up for line 1's fume extraction filter. Maintenance pulled it during scheduled downtime on Friday afternoon and replaced it. Old filter was visibly dark and noticeably heavier than a new one. Restarted the extraction fan after installation and confirmed good airflow before signing off.

After the tech replaced the focus lens on line 3, they put the machine through a full calibration cycle before releasing it back to production. Power meter was set up at the station, readings were taken and logged, and the tech confirmed everything was within spec. Took about 30 minutes total.

Quarterly calibration check on line 6 was due. Machine was pulled from the schedule for about an hour, calibration mode was engaged, power readings taken at the meter station, and the output was verified and confirmed at setpoint. Back in service for the afternoon shift.

PM calendar flagged lubrication on the guide rails for line 4 this week. Maintenance came in during the overlap between shifts, disabled the laser, and worked grease into both the X and Y rails. Ran a test traverse cycle afterwards to distribute it before putting the machine back on the schedule.

Maintenance needed to get inside line 5's machine to replace the beam delivery fiber. Before anyone touched anything, the full energy isolation was done — E-stop pressed, main disconnect thrown at the panel, hasp locked on, personal tag hung. Nobody goes in without seeing that tag. Took about 45 minutes to do the fiber work.

Found a puddle under the chiller on line 1 at the start of second shift — looked like it had been slowly dripping from a hose fitting overnight. About half a liter on the floor. Paused the machine, got a spill kit from the station, soaked it up. Called safety and maintenance. Safety officer came over to verify cleanup.

Someone loaded a powder-coated part on line 3 by mistake — shouldn't have been in the nest at all. It caught during the cut, small flame visible through the window inside the enclosure. Hit the red button immediately, killed the gas valve at the supply panel, called safety. Fire was already out by the time the extinguisher arrived.

Second shift on line 6, the enclosure smoke detector went off during a cut. Couldn't see an open flame through the viewing window but there was definitely smoke building inside. Hit E-stop, killed emission, shut the assist gas at the supply panel. Got safety in before anyone opened the enclosure door.

Line 2, beginning of first shift Monday. Robot ran through the morning checks — powered up the main panel, confirmed coolant level on the chiller was good, verified the gas supply was reading 12 bar at the panel, then enabled emission. Everything in range, machine was ready and cutting by 6:15am.

After the weekend maintenance window on line 5, startup was run Monday morning before production. Coolant level checked out, assist gas was sitting at 11 bar, all pre-checks passed. Emission was enabled and we ran a test cut to verify before releasing the machine to the operators for regular parts.

End of second shift on line 4. Finished the last nest of the run, stopped the cycle, disabled emission, closed off the gas supply at the panel, waited out the 5-minute cooldown per the posted procedure, then powered down main. Everything off by 11pm as scheduled.

Planned maintenance window starting tomorrow meant we had to do a full shutdown on line 1 at end of day today. Stopped the cycle mid-afternoon, disabled emission, shut the assist gas valve, waited the full cooldown period, then hit main power off. Maintenance team was coming in at 6am and needed the machine fully de-energized.

First shift, line 3 unit. We were mid-hold and the number was just slowly backing off — not crashing, just creeping down over maybe a minute and a half. Test eventually flagged it but it took forever to hit the reject point. Tech said it was probably a hairline crack in the part, not our equipment.

Station B by the loading dock, second shift. Hold phase looked okay at first but the readout kept losing ground, real gradual-like. By about forty seconds in it was clearly headed the wrong way. We pulled the part and tossed it in the bin.

Line 4, first shift — everyone on the floor heard it. We were mid-run and the number just vanished. Went from full hold reading to basically nothing in like two seconds flat. Was not a slow thing at all, it just died instantly.

Second shift on line 2, the unit just kept climbing during the charging part of the cycle. Wouldn't stop building — went right through the normal stop point on the display. Alarm kicked before we even got to the stabilization phase.
Bay 3 night shift, the fill portion of the test went way past where it's supposed to level off. The display hit the top of the red zone while it was still charging up. Never even made it to hold.

Third shift, station 2. Fill cycle finished the same as always but we were still sitting way under the target. The hold phase wouldn't even kick in. Maintenance thought it might be the supply line or a bad part — couldn't tell which right away.

Unit near the northeast corner of the floor, afternoon shift. Charge completed on time but the final reading was nowhere near what we need before starting the hold. Tech came over and said supply pressure was suspect upstream.

First shift, station 3. HMI threw a yellow flag on the seal check — one of them came back marginal on the condition readout. But everything was still holding within the acceptable band, no real loss of function. Shift lead said to flag it for the PM crew but keep running for now.

Line 2 second shift. Got a caution-level code on the HMI for one of the seals, said it was reading out of spec on the condition check. Test performance was still inside the acceptance range though. Not a full stop, more of a heads-up type message.

Third shift, line 1 near the window. Big pop from inside the test cell, loud enough to hear over the equipment noise. Chamber went dead instantly, nothing useful on the readout. The main seal had completely given way while the part was under load.

Morning shift, station 2. Unit threw a fault code we hadn't seen in a while — something about the sensor being outside its valid range. We grabbed the reference unit to compare and the readings didn't match by a fair margin. Couldn't trust any of the test results from the last hour.

Line 4 first shift. Transducer was giving a calibration-related error on the HMI. Tech compared it to the secondary gauge and said the primary was reading off by more than it should be. Had to pull testing until maintenance could look at it.

Line 3, afternoon shift. Fixture wouldn't close all the way — kept timing out before it got to the seated position. Part was just loose in there, couldn't run a test. Looked mechanical, not a software hiccup.

End of day on station 1 by the die press. After the test cycle finished the fixture wouldn't let go of the part. Sat there cycling away for what felt like forever. Maintenance had to come over and release it by hand.

Bay 4 night shift. The pressure channel on the HMI just went blank — showing dashes instead of a number. Unit faulted and suspended everything. It was like the sensor just dropped off the network entirely.

Line 2 second shift. Mid-run, the primary readout dropped out completely. No signal, no number, nothing displayed. Unit went into a fault hold and wouldn't continue. Maintenance said it looked like a wiring issue on the transducer side.

First shift, station 3. Heard the pop-off vent open up on the back of the machine — that loud hiss you don't want to hear. Alarm panel lit up with the relief code right after. Supply coming into the station had spiked way over what it should be.

Night shift, line 4. The vent valve on the inlet side let go and started blowing off to atmosphere. Alarm said relief tripped. Compressor upstream was running hot and had pushed the line way too high coming into our station.

First shift, station 2. PM counter hit the limit right at the start of the shift — the display was showing the seal change was due before we could run any more parts. Had to hold up production until the swap was done.

Second shift, bay 2. The little color indicator on the filter housing flipped to red during the routine walk-around. That thing doesn't lie — element was past due. Supply flow was feeling a bit restricted too, just slightly.

Line 2, quality hold at start of week. The calibration sticker on the primary transducer was past its expiry date, and the maintenance planner had it on the schedule. Station pulled offline for the verification check before running any more good parts.

Line 3, morning shift. Clamping stroke was getting noticeably sluggish — taking a lot longer than usual to fully seat. PM board showed the lube interval was due. Maintenance tech came by with the grease cartridge between parts.

Station 2 afternoon shift. Fixture was moving real slow on the closing stroke and our cycle time was creeping up. The PM counter had hit the threshold for the lubrication service. Maintenance took care of it during the next part load.

End of week on line 4, second shift. The sealing surfaces inside the chamber had some gunk and metal chips sitting on them from the week's runs. Had to do the scrub-out before the weekend so Monday morning would start clean.

Weekly walkdown, line 2 first shift. Supply to the station was running about 8 psi over what the setting should be at that time of day. Regulator hadn't been touched but was clearly out of adjustment.

Line 3, first shift maintenance window. Tech needed to get inside the test cell to swap out the internal fittings. Had to do a full energy isolation before anyone went in — locks and tags on the panel, all verified.

Bay 2 morning shift. Supply hose on the back of the unit whipped free while still under full line pressure. Hissing and blowing everywhere, really loud. Nobody was standing near it but we cleared the whole area immediately.

First shift, station 2. Operator noticed something looked off about how the part was sitting in the fixture before the cycle had even stabilized — hit the red button right away. Turned out the part was loaded crooked and would have failed the seal.

Line 3 second shift. A chip of metal fell into the fixture area during a live pressurized cycle. Robot hit the mushroom button immediately without waiting for the automatic fault system to pick it up first.

First shift crew bringing up station 3 on Monday morning after the weekend. Went through the whole bring-up sequence before running any parts — nothing unusual, just checking everything after two days sitting idle.
Line 2 morning startup at shift change. Operator went through the checklist to power up and verify the unit before the first part of the day. Everything looked good coming up.

Last call on second shift, line 4. Went through the close-out on the leak tester before heading home — vent, depressurize, button everything up in the right order. Clean handoff for the third shift crew.

End of night shift, station 1. Had to bring the unit down safely before everyone left. Ran through the sequence to make sure there was no pressure left sitting in the system before the morning crew came in.

Line 3, first shift after the overnight maintenance window. PM crew had finished the seal swap and cleared all their locks. We did the controlled bring-back to make sure everything was right before quality ran a first-article check on it.

Bay 4, second shift. Electrician had been in the panel and released the lockout. Robot ran through the restart check — pulled the lock off, powered up, verified the readouts — then notified the shift supervisor the unit was back and ready.

Line 3 press started dragging bad around 9am on first shift. You could hear it slowing down before it even finished the stroke - felt like it was running out of steam. I hit stop before it stalled out completely. Never tripped, just kept getting slower.

Second shift, about halfway through the bracket run, that big wheel on the side of press 4 was barely turning. Thing was crawling compared to how it sounds at normal speed. We shut it down before it started scrapping parts.

Press 2 went haywire on first shift - that spinning mass started screaming louder than normal. The speed alarm on the panel lit up and I could see the number climbing on the display, way past where it should be. Hit the big red button.

Line 2, mid-morning: the flywheel was absolutely running away on us. Operator hit e-stop because the RPM gauge pegged out at the top of the scale. Never seen it go that fast. Could hear the pitch change from across the cell.

The drive on press 5 fed too much power somehow during a run of door brackets - you could hear the pitch change and then a relay clicked on the panel. Display showed it well above the red line before the alarm went off. Had to call safety.

Press 5 punch timing felt off all morning on line 1. The crank wasn't keeping up with the wheel - you could hear a faint chirp every time it tried to engage. Alarm light came on the panel around 10. Not a stall, just not grabbing right.

Line 1, third shift: every time the operator hit the foot pedal the press would kind of hesitate before the stroke started. Like power was slipping somewhere in the engagement. The crank was turning but not in sync with the flywheel speed.

Press 3 was running real hot on the left side today - caught a burning smell around the brake housing. The machine was completing strokes but it felt like something was fighting the drivetrain. Cycle time was stretched out and the area near the brake got warm to the touch.

Line 4, first shift: the press would complete a stroke but then take way longer to come back around for the next one. Felt like something was dragging on the crank. Strong scorched smell from the drive side of the machine. Nothing stopped it, just slowed it down.

On the big press near dock 2, the ram was moving fine but the cycle time was off by almost half a second per stroke. Like running with the parking brake on, is the best way to describe it. Maintenance found the friction material wasn't fully releasing after the clutch engaged.

Part didn't eject cleanly off the lower die on press 6 and the feed system kicked the next blank in before anyone could react. Material folded over in the tool and locked everything up tight. Had to mash the big red button. Die area was completely stuck.

Line 2, afternoon: a slug got pushed sideways in the cavity and the area sensor went off before the next cycle could start. Press stopped itself but the tooling was locked up solid and wouldn't jog free. Whole line went down.

Lube light came on around 10am and the pressure gauge on the pump box was sitting way down in the yellow zone. Press kept running but the gauge never recovered. Looked like the pump was starving for oil.

Second shift noticed the automatic oiler wasn't distributing - checked the gauge near the pump and it had dropped into the low range. We tried to let it run but couldn't get the reading back up. System wasn't building any pressure at all.

The lube pump on line 1 was working but going nowhere - pressure reading was way up in the red and nothing was coming out at the lubrication points on the machine. Pump motor was straining and the gauge kept climbing. Clearly something was blocked downstream.

Had a weird one on press 6 - lube pump was hammering against something. Tech found a fitting had collapsed inside one of the header lines and nothing could get through. Pressure built up almost to the relief valve. Points were completely dry even with the pump maxed out.

The press tripped out on line 4 mid-run today. The counter on the tonnage screen had gone way past the green zone and the machine just shut off on its own. Overload relay kicked. Turned out a small piece of scrap had gotten back into the die.

Running a bracket job on press 3 and about 200 parts in, the alarm panel lit up and everything stopped. Tonnage readout was showing 680 - way over what the job calls for. The machine just killed itself. Had to reset before we could jog it.

Ran 75 parts before quality caught it - the brackets were coming out thin on one flange, not fully formed. Press never actually tripped or alarmed, just kept running. Went back and checked the tonnage screen and it was reading way lower than the setup sheet calls for all shift.

Line 2, morning: the formed radius on the parts wasn't closing up right. Die setup guy said the slide might have crept up. No alarm went off but when we looked at the tonnage display it was under the normal range - machine never noticed anything was wrong.

Quality pulled a sample from press 5 and found inconsistent coining depth on about 60 pieces. Nothing stopped the machine - it ran the whole batch. When we reviewed the tonnage numbers afterward they were soft all shift, well below spec but no trip at all.

Press 2 quit mid-stroke this morning for no obvious reason. Control screen popped up a position sensor error and the machine locked in place. Couldn't jog it out manually and the control wouldn't let us do anything until maintenance came and reset it.

Line 3 crank stopped in a funny spot partway through a cycle - not at top dead center, not at bottom, just kind of stuck in the middle. The control box was showing a fault about not knowing where the ram was. Took maintenance about 20 minutes to sort it out.

There was a small drip coming from a hose fitting on the tool cooling loop, right side of the die on line 5. Not a lot - maybe a drop every few seconds. Left a small puddle on the bolster plate. Machine was still running fine, nothing alarmed.

Line 5, second shift: coolant level on the reservoir was going down slowly but nothing looked obviously broken. Finally found a weeping connection near the back of the die - slow seep, not spraying. Marked it with a rag for maintenance to address on the next break.

We had a coolant blowout on press 1 this afternoon on line 3. A hose just let go and sprayed fluid everywhere - all over the die, the bolster, the floor around it. Killed the machine immediately. The whole area was soaked in seconds. Nothing gradual about it.

Line 4, first shift: the whole cooling circuit dropped pressure in about two seconds. There was a loud pop and water started pouring out from under the slide - not dripping, pouring. Floor was slick immediately. We hit e-stop and got out of the area.

The stroke counter hit the service mark on line 3 around noon so we stopped to swap the oil drum out. Old drum was reading empty on the sight glass. Pulled it off the reservoir port and rolled in the fresh one during the break window.

Press 4 hit its two-thousand-cycle mark during first shift on line 2 so we stopped it for the scheduled check. Pulled the access cover and looked at the wear tabs on both the clutch disc and the brake lining.

Three-month service was due on the flywheel drive on line 4. Tech came out to do the belt swap and good thing - one of them already had a visible crack running along the inner surface. Would have let go on its own soon.

Line 1, quarterly scheduled downtime for the drive belt change on press 3. Old belts were glazed and one had a chunk missing from the edge. Did the swap and got back into production about 40 minutes later.

Filter gauge on the pump station went into the red during first shift on line 5. Oil was pretty dirty by that point - the element was overdue. Took the pump offline and swapped the cartridge out. Flow came right back up after.

Line 3 lube system: the differential indicator across the filter housing was pinned in the red all morning. Flow was clearly being restricted. Dropped the pump, pulled the cartridge, and it was solid black - completely plugged.

Hit the 250-hour mark on press 2 during second shift so maintenance tagged it for bearing service. Stopped the machine during the lunch break and worked through the grease fittings on the main shaft journal. Quick job.
Line 5, time-based PM came due on the crank bearing lube interval. Brought the grease gun over and hit the nipples on both sides. Took maybe 15 minutes total during the scheduled stop window.

Quality called us out on line 4 this afternoon - the bracket heights were varying too much part to part, all running a bit on the thick side. Die setup had probably drifted up over the course of the shift. Press never flagged anything, just needed the bottom of stroke adjusted.

First shift on press 3, quality tech found about 60 pieces out of tolerance on the wall thickness measurement. The slide must have crept over a few hours of running. Had to stop and look at the shut height position before clearing the parts.

Die change on press 3 after the morning run on line 2. Followed full energy isolation before anyone reached into the tooling area - hasp and personal lock on the main disconnect, tag filled out and signed. Standard process.

Toolmaker needed access to the die on line 5 for a shim adjustment during the break. We stopped the machine, went through full energy isolation before she reached in, personal lock on the disconnect handle. No issues, routine.

There was slippery fluid on the floor on the back side of press 6 right where the counterbalance cylinders are. Oily smell, kind of a yellowish tint - different from cutting fluid. Stopped the machine and got the spill kit before anyone walked through it.

The plant evacuation alarm pulled at 2pm and everyone cleared out. I hit the e-stop on press 5 and killed the main power before leaving the press area. Turned out it was a false pull from the warehouse side but we treated it as real.

Monday morning startup on press 4 - machine had been sitting since Friday third shift. Brought the power up slow and let the lube system build before anyone tried to cycle it. Let the flywheel come up to speed on its own before calling it ready.

Line 2, came in for third shift and the press had been idle all day during a planned downtime. Ran through the morning checks - looked at the pressure readings and confirmed the flywheel was running at normal speed before giving the go-ahead for production.

First shift on line 2, about 0830. The gauge by the booth door was reading low — not by much, just hovering below the lower mark. Airflow felt a little weak when I stood near the intake. Tweaked the damper and watched it creep back up. No parts were scrapped.

Line 1, third shift. Everything was normal and then the draw just died — went to basically nothing in maybe five seconds flat. Fan noise stopped too. Pulled the e-stop right away because we still had mist in the air. Maintenance found the exhaust fan had thrown its belt.

Booth 2, mid-morning first shift. Operators heard a loud thump and the whole booth went quiet — the suction was completely gone, gauge buried at zero almost instantly. Not a slow drift, it just fell off a cliff. Maintenance found a duct connection had blown out on the back side.

Line 3, first shift. The gauge was running high all morning — well above where it's supposed to sit. The exhaust damper felt like it was stuck partially closed. Opened it up and the reading came back down after maybe twenty seconds. Parts near the end of the run had some overspray blow-back.

Second shift over at booth 4. The supply air must have been cranked up too much by the morning crew. Reading was above the top mark. We were seeing light haze inside the enclosure from the restricted exhaust. Opened the damper and it sorted out.

Caught it on the unit by the paint mix room — the booth was running over-pressured, not dangerously but definitely above the top of where it needs to be. No fan failure or alarm, just excessive. Fixed the damper position and monitored for the rest of the shift.

Third shift, line 2. Operator flagged that door panels were coming out with orange-peel texture on the upper third. Checked the atomizer feed line and the air supply was running weak — below where it needs to be. Adjusted the regulator and the texture cleaned up on the next piece.

Booth 1, first shift around noon. The bell cup was spinning but the mist looked chunky to me — not the fine cloud you want. Checked the feed air and it was down. Got it back up with the regulator knob and ran a test piece. Came out clean.

First shift, booth 3. Noticed a slow drip coming off one of the hose fittings on the solvent tank — maybe a few drops per minute onto the floor. No smell in the air and the vapor monitor was quiet. Stopped the pump, threw an absorbent pad under it, and called the maintenance guy over.

Line 2, second shift. A hose on the solvent tank let go all at once — solvent everywhere in seconds. The vapor alarm went off immediately and the smell was strong. We hit the e-stop and fire suppression and got everyone out. Maintenance supervisor called it a complete hose failure at the crimp.

Booth 4, third shift. Heard a pop from inside the booth and then saw a big puddle forming fast under the tank — solvent pouring out. The vapor sensor was screaming within seconds. Hit the big red button, activated suppression, and got out. Fire team came in and cleared the area.

Line 3, first shift. Robot was spraying but the fan looked wrong — narrow on one side, kind of tailing off to the left. Parts on the left edge of the fixture were thin. Paint was definitely still coming out, just not spreading right. Poked it with the clearing needle and it opened back up.

Caught it on the mid-shift check on line 1. The fan was distorted — not gone, but definitely not a clean symmetrical spread. Flow meter was registering non-zero. Clearing needle fixed it in a minute or so and the next test part came out even.

Line 2, third shift. Robot ran its whole spray path but nothing came out of the gun at all. Pump was running fine, pressure was good on the gauge, just zero at the nozzle. Had to pull the tip off and swap it out before we could run again. Old tip was completely packed solid.

Second shift, booth 3. Operator noticed parts coming out of the booth bone dry — not just thin, completely uncoated. Gun wasn't delivering anything. Flow meter read flat zero. Pump pressure was nominal. Replaced the tip and it came right back.

Line 1, first shift Tuesday. The filter panel lit up the yellow indicator — not the red one, just the first level. Nothing stopped running and the parts still looked fine. Noted it in the log and told maintenance to plan a swap during the Thursday downtime window.

Line 3, first shift. The red alarm went off on the exhaust filter — not the yellow, the full alarm. Airflow dropped noticeably and parts were starting to get a haze on them. Had to stop the pump and kill the fan right away. Called the supervisor and plant manager. Emergency change.

Second shift, booth 4. Full alarm on the exhaust filter — completely overwhelmed. You could feel the airflow was gone. Spraying had to stop immediately and the fan went off. When maintenance pulled it the thing looked like a solid mat of overspray. They called it critical.

Maintenance window Thursday morning, line 2. Swapped out the exhaust filter during planned downtime. Old one was dark gray and fully loaded — not in alarm yet but right behind it. New filter in, fan restarted, and the gauge reading dropped back to where it should be.

Booth 1, Friday morning downtime. Came in to do the scheduled exhaust-side filter replacement. The old one was getting up there — not critical but due per the PM sheet. Swapped it out, brought the fan back up, and verified the reading before we started the shift.

Line 3, Tuesday maintenance. Replaced the supply-air filter on the intake side during the downtime window — the makeup-air one, not the exhaust. Old one had a lot of dust on the incoming face. Got the new one in, supply back on, booth reading looked better than it had in a while.

Booth 3, second shift maintenance window. Did the intake filter swap on the fresh-air supply side. Shut the air supply down, pulled the old filter, installed the new one. Booth pressure gauge showed a cleaner reading once we brought supply back up.

Line 2, midweek scheduled clean. Bell cup on booth 1 had visible dried paint around the outer edge — crusty buildup from the previous shift. Stopped the pump, brought it to the cleaning station, soaked it in the cleaning solution, wiped it down. Came off clean and the next test spray looked good.

Booth 4, quality flagged a pattern irregularity that turned out to be dried paint on the spinning cup. Took it through the cleaning routine — soak then wipe. The coating came right off. Pattern was back to normal on the test piece after reinstall.

Line 1, Thursday PM maintenance. PM sheet said the paint pump was due for lube. Stopped it, greased the fittings on the piston side, let it sit, then started it back up. Pump pressure sensor read normal. No issues.

Booth 2, first shift maintenance window. Did the scheduled lube on the paint supply pump. Applied grease to the bearing race per the PM card. Pump restarted fine, pressure reading was right where it should be. Logged it and moved on.

Line 3, quality audit Monday morning. Calibration on the spray tip was overdue. Set up the target panel, did a test fire, and the pattern sensor showed the fan angle was drifting off to one side. Quality engineer reviewed the result and we adjusted before the production shift started.

Booth 1, second shift. Film thickness was coming out with a gradient across parts — heavy on the left, thin on the right. Quality engineer ordered a pattern check. Fired at the calibration panel and the sensor confirmed the fan was skewed. Calibration corrected it.

Line 2, planned maintenance Monday. Before the tech went into the booth to replace a spray arm fitting, we ran the full energy isolation routine — estop first, then main power off, paint supply closed, hasp on, danger tag hung. Tech confirmed zero energy before he stepped inside.

Line 1, second shift. Fire alarm went off inside the booth while we were mid-spray on a door panel batch. Hit the estop, activated suppression, called the fire team, and cleared out. Turned out to be a false alarm from overspray hitting the detector, but we followed the full procedure regardless.

Booth 4, first shift. Operator hit the emergency stop — she saw a flash near the spray arm while it was mid-cycle. Suppression activated and everyone got out. Maintenance found a static discharge had ignited a small vapor pocket. Fire team cleared it before we restarted.

Line 3, second shift. Paint was pooling at the base of the booth during the run — not a huge amount but it was growing. Tank looked intact. Traced it to a drip line that had worked loose at a fitting. Stopped the pump, laid down absorbent pads, got it contained, and called maintenance.

First shift Monday morning, line 2. Robot brought the booth up for the week — main power on, kicked the exhaust fan, waited for everything to settle, checked the pressure reading, then started the pump. Atomizer air read good. Ready to run in about ninety seconds.

Line 3, Tuesday morning startup. Smooth one — power on, fan running, pressure came up clean after the wait, pump on, air pressure good. One of those mornings where everything just works. Logged start time and handed off to production.

End of day shift, line 1. Stopped the pump first, let the booth purge for thirty seconds, then killed the fan and hit the main disconnect. Checked the vapor sensor on the way out — read clean. Let maintenance supervisor know everything was shut down.

Booth 3, end of third shift. Robot ran the shutdown sequence — pump off, purge wait, fan off, main power killed, vapor check. Everything came back clean. Maintenance supervisor confirmed all clear before the shift handed off.

Line 2, second shift. Quality pulled two door skins from the batch and they measured thin — well under the floor spec. The color looked a little translucent, you could almost tell just by looking. Stopped the run, called the quality engineer, and held the parts pending investigation.

Line 3, start of first shift. Did the pre-run cup check and the number was off — drained too fast, paint was thin and watery. Called the paint tech and held the pump before we ran anything. She came and corrected the solvent ratio and re-checked before we went.

Line 4 palletizer started dropping boxes again around 10am on first shift. Every 5 or 6 picks the carton would slip on the way up and land sideways on the pallet. Nothing was alarming loudly but the little vacuum gauge on the pump manifold was reading around 38 when it usually sits at 50-something. Robot kept trying to complete the pick but the grip was weak the whole time.

Line 2 was running fine at the start of second shift then started occasionally missing picks — box lifts halfway and then tilts and gets set back down. The robot was not throwing a hard fault, just retrying over and over. When I checked the vacuum manifold the gauge read 42, definitely below what it should be.

A whole carton came off mid-air on line 3 — robot had it lifted maybe 18 inches off the infeed belt and it just let go instantly. Scared the heck out of the operator standing at the stretch wrapper. The system locked itself out right after the drop and everything went dead. Nothing gradual about it, the carton was there and then it wasn't.

We had an incident on line 1 near end of first shift where a box fell from the arm during the swing. One second the arm was carrying the carton and the next it was on the floor between the infeed and the pallet. The robot went into a hard stop by itself, which is correct, but the carton was crushed at the corner from the drop. The operator said there was no buildup — it went from fine to dropped in one cycle.

I noticed on line 2 the vacuum needle was buried past the 80 mark during second shift — way past where it normally runs. The cups were practically sucking themselves inside out and you could see the top panels of the cartons flexing inward while the arm was holding them.

QC flagged a bunch of cartons coming off line 4 with circular dent marks on the top flap — exactly the size of the suction cups. Checked the gauge at the pump and it was pegged well above where we want it, probably over 85. That much pull is enough to dent the cardboard.

Line 3 palletizer went idle waiting on a pallet for about 4 minutes before the line lead noticed. Two pallets were kind of wedged together at the bottom of the magazine — the bottom one didn't drop clean and the second one got stuck on top of it. The robot was just sitting at home position waiting.

The palletizer near the dock doors kept cycling back to home position and waiting — pallet never showed up at the staging spot. I heard a grinding sound from the dispenser area before the system finally gave up trying to feed one. Stack looks fine from the outside but something is sticking inside the magazine.

Products were piling up on the infeed belt near the gate sensor on line 2 during second shift. The accumulation got so bad a box fell off the side of the conveyor onto the floor. The palletizer just stopped and waited while the upstream line kept sending product.

Second shift said the line went down for about 20 minutes near the end of their run. A box had turned 90 degrees on the conveyor and jammed tight against the guide rail right before the palletizer cell. Everything behind it was backed up solid.

One of the newer operators on line 3 went in through the side gate to retrieve a fallen box while the robot was still in auto. The amber light on the cell started flashing and the HMI beeped — but the robot actually slowed way down rather than stopping hard. She got the box and came out and then it went back to full speed. We got lucky there.

A forklift driver bumped the north guard door with the corner of a pallet load and it swung all the way open. Everything killed instantly — robot arm froze right in the middle of a pick with a carton hanging in the air. The cell was completely dead. Took maintenance about 15 minutes to verify the area and reset it.

Someone ripped the south guard door open hard — we think a pallet edge caught the gate when the fork truck was staging on the dock. All motion stopped immediately and the fault light went solid red. Different from the normal warning — this was a complete lockout, robot didn't move at all even in slow mode.

Robot on line 2 stopped cold mid-cycle and the controller pendant showed an overcurrent fault code on axis 3. Nothing obvious to look at from the outside but the drive cabinet had a red LED flashing on the third slot. Robot wouldn't jog or home, just sat there faulted.

During startup this morning on line 1 the arm started to home and then seized up after about 10 degrees of travel on the wrist axis. Error on the pendant pointed to an encoder feedback problem on joint 4. Drive cabinet light was solid red on that slot.

Line 4 palletizer threw a fault halfway through second shift — arm was in the middle of placing a carton and just stopped moving. Screen on the controller showed an axis fault with an overcurrent code. Nothing was physically jammed, the arm just refused to move and the drive cabinet was showing a red indicator.

The HMI on line 3 went blank for about 30 seconds and came back with a communication loss message at the top. The robot was just sitting there doing nothing even though all the conveyor lines upstream were still running and sending product. No alarm sound, no motion, just a silent stop.

Line 4 palletizer dropped offline around 2pm — no estop pressed, no alarm horn, just stopped cold. Maintenance checked and found the Ethernet cable at the back of the robot controller was barely seated — looks like it got nudged loose. Reseating it brought everything back.

Third shift reported that the palletizer by the loading dock went into what they described as a frozen state — no faults on the HMI except a small blinking comm indicator in the corner. Robot was not faulted, not in estop, just not doing anything. PLC side showed the connection to the robot as offline.

The pump on line 1 was hot enough that I didn't want to keep my hand on it for more than a second. The amber caution light on the panel was lit but the machine hadn't stopped yet — it finished the cycle it was on and then paused. Maintenance said it had been running continuously for most of the shift with no breaks.

Maintenance tech said the pump on line 2 was working harder than usual — motor sounded like it was straining and the pickup force on the cartons felt sluggish. Pulled the inlet filter and it was completely grey and packed with fine carton dust. Could barely see daylight through it.

The 500-hour PM tag on line 1 was overdue by about 50 hours based on the runtime log. When we finally pulled the filter during the weekend shutdown it had so much fines and fiber on it that we couldn't blow air through it with the shop gun.

Line 4 pump differential pressure started spiking on the HMI trend screen — way above the 15 mark. The pump was audibly working harder between picks. Filter ended up being absolutely loaded with paper fiber from the new carton stock we switched to last week — apparently it sheds a lot more than the old material.

Joint 3 on the line 2 robot was making a high-pitched squeak on every back-swing cycle — you could hear it from the other side of the building. PM log showed we were about 300 hours past the greasing interval. Nobody had flagged it because the robot was still picking fine.

During the morning walkthrough on line 4, the maintenance tech heard a low grinding sound from the elbow area on the arm during auto cycle. Checked the service log and last documented grease was over 2200 hours ago. Definitely overdue.

Robot on line 3 was dropping maybe 1 in every 200 boxes — not enough to shut it down automatically but the rejects were piling up fast. Looked at the end-of-arm tool during a break and two of the four cups were cracked around the rim and one had a chunk missing from the lip.

The dispenser on line 3 was making a chattering noise at the start of every pallet cycle — kind of a tick-tick-tick sound from the drive side. Looked at the chain and it was visibly dry, no lube sheen at all.

The light curtain on the north gate of the line 2 cell was intermittently triggering zone clear faults — maybe once every couple of hours — without anyone actually being near the fence. No actual intrusion, just random false trips. Signal strength test showed the receiver was marginal.

After the afternoon product changeover to the smaller SKU on line 2, the new boxes were coming off the pallet with black smudge marks on the top flap right where the cups contact them. Old label adhesive had built up thick on the gripper face plate and was transferring onto the new product.

End of third shift the cups on line 4 had a visible ring of brown cardboard dust around the lip edge. The arm was still picking without drops but the QC supervisor raised a product cleanliness concern and flagged it for the shift change log.

Maintenance needed to get inside the work envelope on line 3 to replace the pallet dispenser guide rail — totally inaccessible from outside the fence. We had to do the full energy isolation at the main disconnect before anyone stepped through the gate. Tagged and tested before entry.

Technician on line 1 found a broken proximity sensor bracket inside the cell — bracket had sheared and was hanging loose near the robot path. Couldn't reach it from outside the fence so we had to isolate power and go in. Full lockout procedure was done before entry, confirmed dead at the panel before anyone touched anything.

Found a puddle under the vacuum pump on line 4 — maybe a cup or so of pump oil on the concrete. Slippery enough that someone could have gone down on it walking past. Forklift driver almost rolled through it.

Operator on line 3 hit the red button when she saw the arm swinging toward her — she had reached into the edge of the area to grab a fallen carton and didn't realize the robot was mid-cycle. Everything froze instantly. Arm was stopped with a carton in the gripper about 3 feet off the ground.

First shift couldn't get the line 1 palletizer to go into auto mode this morning. The HMI was up, robot had power, but it just sat there and wouldn't accept the cycle start. Turned out the vacuum pump hadn't had enough time to build pressure after power-on and the system was waiting on a sensor confirm before it would let the robot move.

End of second shift the line lead on line 4 forgot to send the robot home before cutting power at the main disconnect. When first shift came in the next morning the arm was sitting mid-air between the infeed and the pallet position. The system wouldn't accept a normal power-on sequence — it just kept asking for a home confirmation.

Outgoing third shift left two cartons sitting on the infeed belt when they shut down line 2. When first shift powered up in the morning the robot immediately tried to pick the first one before a pallet was staged. It threw a fault right away and had to be manually cleared before normal startup could continue.

QC rejected a pallet from line 2 at the end of second shift — one full layer was rotated 90 degrees from the pattern spec. The stretch wrapper had already done half a wrap before the QC tech caught it on the exit conveyor. Had to cut the film and manually re-stack that layer.

Second shift on line 4 — parts coming out of the washer looking greasy. Checked the spray arms and they were barely putting out anything. Gauge on the side of the machine was sitting at 8 PSI, way down from the usual 25. Pump is still spinning, it just is not pushing.

Third shift noticed the cleaning side was not keeping up. Pushed through a batch of valve bodies and they came out with residue on the machined surfaces. Glanced at the pressure indicator — it was barely touching 12 PSI. Pump running fine, just not making pressure like it should.

Line 2 washer — red light came on the panel around 2 PM. Something is backing up downstream; the gauge is pegged past 45 and still climbing. Never seen it that high before. The pump sounds like it is straining under the load.

Mid-cycle on line 3, the spray just cut out completely — zero. Not low, totally gone. Machine did not fault, the conveyor kept moving parts through, but nothing was coming out of the nozzles at all. Happened in about two seconds flat.

We were running a clean cycle and then gone — no wash at all. The gauge went from 22 to nothing in one shot. E-stop was not hit, controls look normal, pump seems like it is trying to run but there is zero output pressure.

Parts are coming through with an oily film. Checked around and found the tank temp is only sitting at 128 degrees — been there for about 20 minutes. The heater light is showing active on the panel but the bath is barely warm.

Line 1, morning shift. The water in the tank feels barely warm through the inspection glass. Temperature display was showing 135, setpoint is 155. Heater is apparently running but the reading keeps drifting down instead of recovering.

Steam started coming off the tank on line 3. The alarm horn went off — temp gauge is showing 192 degrees. Well past where it is supposed to be. The whole area around the unit is getting hot and humid.

The float alarm beeped on line 2. Walked over and looked through the sight glass — you can barely see any fluid in there. Level indicator is flashing on the panel. Looks like it is down maybe 40 percent or more below the fill mark.

Line 3, afternoon shift. Pressure gauge looked completely normal but parts were coming out dirty on one side. Stopped the machine and looked through the inspection door — one whole bank of spray arms was bone dry while the others were flowing fine.
Red fault light came on the main panel on line 1 — the overload indicator is solid. Machine stopped mid-cycle. The motor area smells a bit hot. Looks like the pump thermal trip popped.

Line 3 washer went down with a fault. The overload relay on the motor control cabinet is tripped. Pump was sounding labored for a few minutes before it cut out, then the breaker popped and everything stopped.

The differential pressure across the filter housing is reading 13 PSI. Maintenance said it has been creeping up all week. Time to swap it out — screen is probably loaded with metal fines from the last batch of castings we ran.
Scheduled PM on the south washer — per the maintenance log it has been 510 hours since the last filter swap. No alarm is on yet but we are pulling the cartridge per the hour-based interval.

Weekly PM on line 2 washer. No fault and no alarm — just time on the calendar to pull the nozzle assemblies and clean the mineral scale off. Spray pattern looked a bit uneven during last Thursday's run but no flow was lost.

Monthly PM on line 1 — need to drain the tank and get the sludge out. There is a visible layer of grey sediment on the bottom through the inspection port and it has been over 30 days since the last full drain.

The washer by the stamping press is due for its monthly cleanout. We can see black sediment buildup on the inside of the sight glass and the drain plug has not been touched since last cycle. Scheduling a full drain and scrub.

Quality flagged the washer on line 3 — parts are failing the downstream cleanliness check and the lab titrated the bath at 1.8 percent detergent, way below spec. The solution looks almost clear. Needs chemical added today.

The 1000-hour PM interval hit on the south washer pump. Maintenance log shows the bearings have not been greased since last quarter. No symptoms yet, but scheduling it out for this weekend before the interval gets any further past.

Monthly belt inspection on line 3 — found a 4-inch crack along one of the belt seams near the middle section. Belt is also stretching too much and not tracking right through the wash zone. Needs to come out.

Line 1 washer conveyor belt has a frayed edge that has been getting progressively worse. Caught it during this morning's walkaround. The belt is also sagging in the middle section and catching slightly on the guide rail.

Maintenance is going in to replace the spray nozzle manifold on line 4. Need to lock the machine out before anyone gets near the internals — can not have that pump or the conveyor kick on while someone has their hands inside.

Tech is climbing into the tank on the south washer to hand-scrub the sludge off the bottom. Full energy isolation is required before anyone steps inside the enclosure. Can not touch it until everything is locked and tagged.

Line 2 washer — maintenance needs to reach inside the hood to clear a part that wedged itself on the conveyor track. Machine has to be fully de-energized before anyone puts a hand in there. Setting up the hasp now.

There is a puddle forming outside the containment pan on line 4 — looks like it came from a fitting at the back of the machine. Fluid is running toward the center aisle drain and getting close to the yellow walk line.

The fill alarm on the detergent day tank went off on line 3. Level indicator is showing over 95 percent capacity and the fill valve was apparently left open after the last top-up. No spill yet but the tank is about to run over.

Someone hit the red mushroom button on the line 2 washer — everything stopped, nothing is moving. We need to figure out which e-stop was activated and twist it out before we can even attempt to restart the machine.

E-stop got bumped on the east washer, probably by a forklift passing too close to the panel. All motion stopped mid-cycle. Parts are sitting inside the wash zone. Need to clear the e-stop and do a controlled restart.

First shift, coming in Monday morning after the weekend. The washer on line 1 has been cold since Friday afternoon. Need to bring it up properly — warm the bath to operating temp, check the level, get the pump going before we start loading parts.

End of day on line 2. Production is done and we need to shut the washer down right — stop the conveyor first, then the pump, then the heater, then kill the main. Do not want the pump running dry or the bath boiling overnight.

Third shift wrapping up at the east unit. Time to shut down for the two-day weekend. Pump and heater need to come off in the right order to avoid any problems over the long idle. Following the sequence on the placard.

Quality hold called on line 1 — the bearing housings coming out of the washer have a visible oily sheen when you hold them up to the light at the right angle. Need to pull a sample and evaluate before we send any more downstream.

Daily quality check on line 2 washer — pulling a cup of bath solution to run through the conductivity meter and confirm we are still inside spec. No symptoms, no complaints from production, just the routine morning verification.

Line 3 plasma table threw a warning about ten minutes into the cut program on first shift. Gauge on the supply panel was reading low, somewhere around 75 PSI when it should be up in the 90s. Cut stopped itself. We jogged the supply valve up a bit and checked the reading again before restarting. Didn't call it in but noted it in the log.

Unit by the east wall started lagging during long cuts — you could hear the arc sputtering and the cut surface looked rougher than normal. Checked the panel and the supply was starved down, had maybe 78 PSI showing. Wasn't a blowout or anything dramatic, just crept down over the shift. Second shift had to address it before restart.

The plasma table near bay 4 tripped an alarm mid-shift. Display was showing an over-pressure warning, and the supply line gauge was way up past 125 PSI. Hit the shutoff on the gas panel and backed off the supply. Didn't see any line damage but called maintenance to inspect the regulator before we touched it again.

First shift, the big plasma cutter by the loading dock kept alarming out every time we tried to run. Checked the gas panel and everything was pushed way high — over 120 on the supply gauge. Had to shut down the gas feed entirely and vent the line before maintenance could get in. They found the regulator was stuck open.

The cutter on line 2 just died mid-cut — not a slow fade, it literally dropped out instantly. Checked the gas panel right after and the supply was at nothing, maybe 8 PSI. Hit the E-stop and shut the gas line down hard. Something in the supply ruptured — called maintenance and the supervisor right away, didn't try to restart.

Near end of shift on line 5 the cutter dropped pressure in seconds — I was watching the HMI and the PSI just fell off a cliff, not a gradual creep. Had to slam the estop and close the supply valve at the panel. Whole section smelled a little off afterward. Supervisor was on-site within two minutes and we locked it out.

Running the morning job on the line 1 table and heard a clunk — torch grazed the sheet on a pierce. The THC screen was showing the standoff way below where it should be, around 0.04 inches or so. Had to pause the program and jog the torch up manually before continuing. Left a small gouge on one part; inspector flagged it.

Torch was physically dragging on the material during lead-in on thick plate — you could see it making contact. Standoff reading on the controller was basically zero. Operator paused the cycle and nudged the height back up incrementally. First two parts from that nest got flagged by QC because of the drag marks.

Parts from the afternoon run on line 3 had terrible bevel on the cut edges — way more than spec allows on any of them. Looked at the THC log and the torch was riding too high the whole time, standoff around 0.30 inches. Arc was clearly stretching. Had to jog it down and rerun a test piece before releasing the next nest.

The plasma table near the east dock started producing parts with heavy dross on the top face and a rounded top edge on every cut. Ran a standoff check and the reading was over 0.28 inches — torch sitting too far off the plate. Looks like the THC wasn't tracking the plate surface properly. Paused the run and pulled the height back in before continuing.

The plasma supply unit over on line 4 started flashing a yellow indicator about halfway through the shift. Checked the readout on the power supply box and the coolant temp was sitting at 48 degrees C. Paused the cut, let it sit, checked the reservoir — level looked okay but temperature was still climbing. Brought in maintenance to check the cooling loop.

Plasma cutter was cutting sluggish and derated itself to lower power on second shift without throwing an arc fault. Display was showing a thermal warning — the coolant temp readout on the power supply was past the 45 mark. Operator paused and maintenance checked the coolant loop. No leak, just ran hot from a long continuous job without break time.

Line 2 plasma table kept failing to start this morning. Tried to resume the job three times and each time it just clicked repeatedly — no arc transfer to the plate. Machine locked itself out after the third attempt. Called maintenance to pull the consumables and check. Electrode looked completely eroded down to nothing.

During the material changeover on second shift, the torch wouldn't establish an arc on the new nest at all. Machine threw a fault code after several attempts. Maintenance opened the torch cap and found the nozzle was blown out — orifice completely deformed. Gas supply was fine, power was fine, it was strictly a consumable issue.

Third shift on line 5 — pilot arc kept cycling three times each attempt but never transferred to the workpiece. Could hear it trying to fire and failing. Checked the arc voltage readout and it wasn't reaching transfer threshold. Maintenance swapped the electrode and nozzle and the machine fired up on the first try after that.

The gantry on the big table in bay 3 stopped dead in the middle of a long cut. Y-axis just froze mid-traverse. Drive cabinet was showing a fault light, servo drive had tripped. Hit the E-stop and called maintenance — they reset the drive fault and verified the encoder wiring before we could get back to running.

On line 1, the cutter started tracing a curve where the program called for a straight line — X-axis was hunting and oscillating. Then it stopped altogether with a fault code on the servo panel. Encoder must have lost signal partway through the cut. Maintenance had to clear the fault and verify both axes tracked correctly before sign-off.

Parts coming off the line 3 plasma table have been looking rough all morning — heavy slag buildup on the bottom edge of every cut and the kerf looks ragged instead of clean. Maintenance checked the arc-on timer and it was over 3 hours on these consumables. Time to swap electrode and nozzle before the next nest.

The downdraft on the line 4 table has been struggling all day — fumes aren't clearing fast enough and you can smell the smoke hanging around the cutter. Checked the differential pressure gauge on the dust collector and it was reading well above the normal range. Filter has to be swapped before this shift ends.

Second shift noticed the exhaust from the downdraft unit near bay 2 smelled unusually heavy — way more fume than usual making it past the hood. Maintenance checked the filter housing and the pressure differential was over 2 inches WC above baseline. Pulled the cartridge and put a fresh one in. Extraction improved immediately.

Gantry on the line 1 table has been making a low grinding noise on the Y-axis for the last couple of hours. Not a fault, not stopping the machine, just noise that wasn't there yesterday. Maintenance checked the rails and they were bone dry — over 40 hours since the last grease cycle. Worked the lube gun down both axes.

Periodic PM came up on the east-wall plasma table. Cut quality wasn't the issue and no alarms, but the maintenance log showed the rails and rack hadn't been greased since the counter hit 38 hours. Greased the rack and linear rails on both X and Y before any wear started showing up in the cuts.

Parts from the morning run on line 5 are showing inconsistent standoff across the sheet — leading edge of the cut looks fine but by the time the torch gets to the far side, the kerf angle changes noticeably. THC controller also threw a drift warning overnight. Called for a recalibration before loading the next nest.

After the torch assembly was replaced on line 2 last night, the standoff has been inconsistent across the table. Reads differently at the front versus the back of the cutting envelope — same program, same material, different results by position. Ran the calibration routine on the controller to re-establish the baseline across the full travel.

The water table on the line 3 plasma cutter is packed with slag — buildup is past the slat height and parts were sitting in sludge when I pulled them this morning. Dross sticking to the bottom of the plate more than usual. Need to drain and scrape before the next shift can run good parts.

Maintenance log flagged the 80-hour service interval on the east-side table this afternoon. Water level was high and the debris layer was thick — looked like slag had been accumulating since before the last weekend. Drained the table during the lunch window and cleared out the buildup from the slat bed.

Operator on second shift reported a faint smell near the back of the line 4 table — not strong, could be nothing, but it was definitely there when you stood close to the gas panel area. Maintenance walked the supply lines with a sniffer wand and checked all the fittings. Found a loose compression fitting at one junction near the regulator.

Thirty-day inspection came due on the plasma table by the loading dock. No issues reported from operators all month, but we walked the supply lines with the detector wand anyway per the schedule. One section near the secondary regulator showed a faint positive reading. Tightened the fittings and re-checked before logging clear.

Maintenance was scheduled to replace the torch lifter mechanism on line 2 before first shift. Before anyone touched any hardware, we ran through the energy isolation: hit the estop, threw the main disconnect, hung the hasp and danger tag per procedure. Three people on the job and all three added personal locks to the hasp.

Power supply on the east-side plasma table needed the internal capacitor bank inspected — full energy isolation required before anyone opened the enclosure. LOTO applied at the main breaker with hasp and danger tag before the maintenance tech went in. Verified zero energy state with a meter before proceeding with the inspection.

Small fire broke out on the cutting table on line 3 during a thick plate run — a scrap piece trapped under the slats caught from a large dross ball that landed on it. Smoke detector went off. Operator hit the estop and killed the downdraft fan immediately to stop feeding air to it, then grabbed the extinguisher from the wall. Supervisor called right away.

A forklift came too close to the plasma table on line 4 while it was actively cutting — operator hit the red estop on the panel as a precaution. Not a machine fault, strictly a personnel clearance issue. Arc dropped and the gantry stopped where it was. Supervisor came over and cleared the area, then they reset and resumed once the forklift was clear.

A new trainee walked into the restricted zone on line 2 while the cutter was running — floor operator hit the nearest estop button immediately without hesitation. Machine halted, arc off, gantry stopped mid-path. After the trainee was escorted out, supervisor assessed the situation, confirmed the reset, and verified machine status before restarting.

There's a puddle of coolant working its way out from under the plasma unit on line 5 — probably a couple of gallons on the concrete between the machine and the operator panel. Flagged the area and called the supervisor before it could spread into the main aisle between the machines.

Came in first shift and the plasma table on line 1 was fully powered down from the previous night's shutdown. Had to walk through the full power-up in order: main disconnect, then the plasma supply, wait for it to initialize, verify the gas pressure was in range before calling it ready. Took about three minutes before the system was stable enough to run a test cut.

Monday morning after a full weekend shutdown — the line 3 plasma cutter was cold and completely de-energized. Maintenance walked through the startup: threw the main power, brought up the plasma supply unit, waited for the ready indicator, and verified the gas pressure was in spec before the operator loaded the first nest of the week.

End of second shift on the line 4 plasma table — ran through the shutdown steps before leaving. Paused the cut program, powered down the plasma supply, closed the gas feed at the panel, then opened the main disconnect and left it open. Left a note in the log confirming the shutdown was clean before clocking out.

Inspector pulled a sample from the line 2 plasma table nest after the morning run and found heavy bottom dross on roughly half the parts. Kerf width was also measuring wider than the spec tolerance on the thin-gauge sections. Quality hold placed on the whole batch until the root cause is identified and corrected.

First shift line 3 — inspection after the first nest showed dross only on one side of all the parts, not across the board. Bottom edge looked clean on the left side but loaded up heavily on the right side of every part. Measured the kerf width and it wasn't consistent across the table. Quality called for a full inspection before releasing any parts from the next run.

After maintenance replaced the torch assembly on line 2 last night, the first test cut this morning showed a consistent angular bevel that shouldn't be in the program. Looks like the torch isn't sitting square in the mount. Going to verify the perpendicularity with a gauge and re-datum to the table surface before running any production parts.

The torch on line 4 got bumped by a part shift during a heavy plate job — heard a solid bang and the next cut was noticeably off angle. Cut angles were deviating from spec. Homed the torch and ran the squareness check against the table surface. Torch was slightly cocked in the holder. Readjusted and confirmed the height sensor reading was stable before resuming.

Line 2, second shift. The cure zone on the big oven has been running about 15 degrees cold for the past ten minutes or so. Parts coming out look okay so far but I'm not comfortable with that gap sitting there. No alarms tripped, just a steady creep down from where we normally sit all shift.

Noticed the temp gauge on Zone 1 has been lagging the recipe for a good while now — sitting maybe 18 degrees short of where it needs to be. No bangs, no alarms, no sudden anything, just quietly drifted down from the start of the shift. Checked it twice, same reading both times.

Zone 1 just cratered. Went from 385 down to under 310 in less than two minutes. Nothing gradual about it — whole zone went cold fast. You could watch the number just fall. Burner must have gone out on us.

The oven temp on the cure zone took a nosedive right around the 10am break. Product was still in there, too. Went from normal operating range way below setpoint so fast I honestly thought the display was busted at first, but it's real — you can feel the heat difference at the exit.

Zone 1 went past 410 degrees. We're supposed to be capped at 400. Display read 414 for a couple of minutes before I caught it. Parts were running through there — they might be cooked. Need to flag that batch.

Oven ran hot this morning on line 4 — Zone 1 hit 408 degrees, which is over our max. Product was in-process when it happened. I pulled what I could off the exit end when I saw the gauge reading but those parts that went through at peak need to be put on hold.

Saw Zone 1 display showing 406 and still climbing before anyone acted. Ceiling's 400. Parts were in the oven the whole time. Temp kept going up for a bit before it leveled. Could be overcured parts in that run.

Tried to bring the west oven up at the start of first shift this morning and the burner just won't catch. It goes through the whole ignite sequence, you hear the click, and then nothing happens. Tried it twice manually. No flame.

Morning startup on line 3 oven, burner just won't light. Sequence runs like normal, you hear the clicking, but the flame detector is showing nothing. Second attempt same result. Oven is sitting cold and we've got product waiting.

The conveyor on the powder coat oven seems sluggish today — not stopped, still moving, but parts are taking noticeably longer to come out the other end. Speed looks maybe 20% under where it needs to be when I timed a part through. No alarm, no fault, just dragging.

Line 4 conveyor belt running noticeably slow — you can stand there and watch it and tell it's not at production pace. No alarm has tripped, no full stop, but it's definitely not running right. Been like this maybe 15-20 minutes since we loaded up the first rack.

Second shift, line 3. Belt's technically moving so no fault light came on, but it's clearly not keeping up with pace. Parts are dwelling longer in the hot zone than they should. Been going slow for about 20 minutes by my count.

Conveyor on the cure oven completely locked up on us. Drive motor is running — you can hear it humming — but the belt isn't moving at all. Got product sitting in the oven right now while this thing is stuck.

Belt stopped dead in the middle of a production run. Motor sounds like it's still trying to turn it. Something's jammed it hard because the belt isn't going anywhere. Parts are sitting in the hot zone. Full stop — not slow, just zero movement.

Line 2 oven conveyor quit moving entirely during third shift. The control panel shows it's commanded to run, drive says it's on, but nothing is happening. Completely still. Not a slow-down situation — this thing is stopped cold.

The exhaust system on the cure oven seems weak this week. The pressure gauge is sitting in the yellow band — not red, not alarming — but it's been slowly trending down since yesterday's shift. Fumes are smelling a little stronger in the area around the oven entry.

Noticed the exhaust pressure reading below the green zone on the panel by the west oven. Fan's still running fine, no fault code, no alarm, just sitting in the caution range. Been there since start of shift as far as I can tell.

Exhaust pressure alarm went off on the panel by the loading dock oven. Reading is way above normal — not low, way too high. The fan motor sounds like it's straining. Something must be blocking the duct downstream.

Faint smell of gas over by the cure oven on the east side of the plant — not strong, but it's definitely there if you walk close to the burner cabinet. The gas detector panel isn't alarming but it's reading a little above zero. Been like this for about ten minutes now.

GAS ALARM going off on the cure oven row — high-level alarm, not a caution. Strong smell in the area, detector is in the red zone. This is not a trace whiff, this is the big one. People are already clearing out of the bay.

The gas concentration alarm is screaming on line 2. Detector reading over the emergency threshold — you can really smell it strong now. We need to get everyone out and shut it all down. This is not a minor thing.

Emergency gas alarm activated in the cure oven bay on the north side. Detector is pegged at high, full alarm condition flashing. Could smell it before the alarm even went off. Evacuating the floor now — this is serious, way more than just a trace reading.

The DP gauge on the exhaust filter housing by the east oven has been in the red zone for two days now. Put a work order in but nobody's come to swap it yet. That filter is well past the swap-out mark and the exhaust is starting to run sluggish.

Exhaust filter on line 3 oven is loaded up — differential pressure indicator is right at the replace-now mark and it's been sitting there since yesterday. Getting close to a week overdue on PM for this one. Need new media in there.

Belt on the cure oven conveyor has been drifting to one side — you can clearly see it running off-center when you watch it from the tail end. Weekly inspection is overdue too. Might just be a tension or alignment issue but it needs a look.

Conveyor belt on the east oven is wandering to the right side of the track. Not jammed, belt's still moving, just not tracking straight. Can hear it rubbing a little on the frame guide on the right side when it comes around the tail pulley.

Combustion on the line 1 oven burner is looking off — flame is yellowish and kind of lazy instead of the clean blue we normally see. We're already on the monthly PM schedule for the nozzle this week anyway. Probably fouled up with carbon.

Burner efficiency has been dropping on the north oven this week. Flame color is not the usual tight blue pattern — it's irregular and dirty-looking. Overdue on the monthly nozzle cleaning too. Running past the PM date on that one.
