A metal chip ejected out of the joint gap at the end of a rundown and pinged off the guarding panel right near the operator position. Operator slapped the red mushroom button on station 4 immediately and the whole cell went down hard. Supervisor came over to look before anyone touched the reset.

Line 2 torque station dropped into an e-stop during a rundown cycle — tool locked mid-stroke and everything stopped. Nobody hit a button manually; it tripped on its own. Maintenance thinks a safety relay in the control cabinet kicked it out on an internal fault. Called it in and waited for the all-clear from supervision before resetting.

Second shift on line 1: someone's jacket sleeve caught the palm safety button right next to the torque fixture and the whole cell hard-stopped mid-cycle. Took about 20 minutes to sort out who needed to authorize the reset and get everyone clear of the zone before we could bring it back up.

A new operator from the training group walked right into the robot work zone at station 8 while it was still in auto mode — the area scanner detected the break and killed all motion immediately. Nobody got hurt but we stopped the whole line and did a headcount and area sweep before calling it safe.

A material handler tried to reach in past the light curtain to grab a finished part while the robot arm was still completing the last torque cycle. Safety scanner tripped and everything stopped hard. Supervisor and the safety coordinator were both notified before we even thought about resetting anything.

First shift startup on line 3 this morning: the pressure readings looked low on the initial check — took about three minutes after the main air valve opened before everything stabilized in the normal range. Held off on releasing to production until the readings sat steady for a couple minutes.

Monday morning startup at station 7 coming back from the long weekend: the controller had lost its date and time setting after the power interruption Friday night. The startup sequence was throwing a configuration fault and would not advance past the initialization screen until we reset the clock.

End of day shift on line 4 last Thursday: the operator closed up and just killed the main breaker without running the shutdown sequence first. Came in next morning and found a part still clamped tight in the fixture with the nutrunner parked on top of it. No damage luckily but had to manually release the clamp.

Third shift wrapping up station 2 last night: the shutdown log printout jammed in the printer so we could not get the paper confirmation of close-out. Maintenance had to come over and physically verify the unit was fully de-energized and clear before they would sign off and release the area to housekeeping.

QE ran a mid-week sample pull on line 3 finished assemblies on Wednesday afternoon — grabbed 10 pieces from the outbound rack and put them on the audit bench. Two of them were sitting right at the low edge of the acceptance window but still technically passing. Logged the data and flagged the trend for the weekly review.

During the Friday afternoon audit on station 5 output, the bench audit transducer was showing values consistently about 2 Nm above what the station controller had been logging for those same parts. That kind of discrepancy between the station and the bench tool does not just happen on its own. Kicked it to engineering.

Controller on line 2 flagged a bunch of parts from the afternoon run where the angle trace shows a step in the curve — it winds normally then kind of catches and jumps forward. That step pattern is a classic cross-thread signature. Parts got pulled and tagged before the end of shift.

Station 11 logged three consecutive high-angle rejects early this morning. The fastener was going in fine by feel and hitting the target torque number just fine, but the angle counter was running way too many degrees before the torque started building. Wrong fastener length ended up being in the supply bin — shorter shank than the job called for.

Near the end of second shift on line 4, the angle encoder was logging values well over the program limit even on parts that were hitting their torque target just fine. Engineering thinks the joint crush rate was off on this batch of brackets — sent the whole pallet for a teardown inspection to understand what is actually happening in the joint.

Checked on the cleaner at station 4 around 9 AM and the bath felt cool. Looked at the gauge — it was sitting at 48 degrees when we run it at 55. Parts coming out with a light oily film. Nothing alarmed out, just reading low for a while.

Second shift here, the unit by bay 7 was only at 50°C when I checked around 2 AM. No fault codes, no lights, just the thermometer sitting low. Bumped the heat up and it crept back to normal over the next half hour.

The south-side wash unit has been 6 degrees under target all morning. No alarms firing. Parts aren't coming out as bright as they should — the residue you normally don't see is showing up on the inspection stand.
We were mid-run and the bath temp just fell off a cliff — lost 12 degrees in under two minutes. Nothing gradual about it. Think the element gave out. Hit pause immediately and called maintenance.

Right around 6:30 on first shift the cleaner near the unload dock went from 54 down to 41 degrees in what felt like seconds. It was not a slow drift. Killed the cycle and got the tech out — heater died mid-run.
The high-temp alarm went off on the cleaner near press 3. Panel was flashing, readout showed 68°C. Had to stop the run — nothing should be operating anywhere near that hot.
During a changeover the unit near station 9 had the overheat indicator on and the temp was at 66°C. Had to pull the parts already in the tank and hold the batch until it came back down to safe range.

The sight glass on the cleaner at the end of line 2 was showing the fluid sitting pretty low — call it three-quarters. Yellow warning light was on but the transducers were still covered. Topped it off and kept running.
Came in between shifts for a walk-around and the level indicator on the corner unit was blinking amber. Fluid looked low in the glass but nothing was exposed. Added chemical and the light cleared.

Fluid dropped so far you could see the tops of the transducer plates in the unit by the rinse station. The ultrasonics were making a high-pitched rattling sound I've never heard before. Killed the power to the transducers right away.

The fill line on the south dock cleaner must have been blocked overnight. By 10 AM the tank was about half full with ultrasonics still going. Parts weren't even fully submerged. Had to stop and refill before continuing.

Noticed a slow drip coming from one of the fittings on the side of the cleaner near bay 5. Maybe a few drops per minute. Nothing major, no puddle on the floor. Put a rag under it and left a note for maintenance.

The elbow joint on the return line at the back of the unit has a weep going. Been watching it for an hour and it hasn't gotten worse. Dripping into the berm, not onto the floor, but the seep is definitely real.

The whole side seam of the cleaner near the loading dock just let go. Fluid was everywhere — had to get everyone away from the area immediately. Floor sensor alarm was screaming. We hit the red button and evacuated that corner of the shop.

A drain-side pipe blew completely during the noon run on line 3. We're talking a serious flood situation, not a drip. The berm was overwhelmed. Called out a full area evacuation and got safety on the radio.

The cleaner by the loading dock dumped almost its entire tank onto the plant floor in about 30 seconds flat. The containment couldn't handle it. We hit estop, cleared the area, and notified the supervisor and the safety officer.

Fault light on the generator box lit up on the unit in cell 3 and the panel showed a transducer error code. No weird sounds, no heat, just the alarm and a solid red LED. Shut down the ultrasonics and logged it.

Mid-run on line 6 the control panel threw a transducer alarm — looked like an electrical fault based on the code displayed. The machine stopped itself but I powered down the generator manually as well and called the tech.

The frequency readout on the unit by the rinse tank was sitting at 43.5 kHz all morning. No error code on the panel, just the gauge reading high. Cleaning results were noticeably off — parts coming out with more residue than usual.

The overload alarm on the power supply went off on the cleaner near press 8 but there was no transducer fault showing anywhere. Generator box felt hot to the touch. Tripped once, reset it, held for ten minutes then tripped again.
The generator box on the corner cleaner alarmed out — overload indicator lit up but transducer check came back clean, no shorts or opens. Had to cycle the reset twice before it would stay up.

During second shift the power unit on the unit by bay 2 started running louder than normal, then the overload light came on. No transducer codes. Reset it once and it held, but maintenance wants to look at the generator.

Weekly flush was due on the unit at station 4. The fluid had gone dark brownish and smelled off — wasn't going to clean anything properly in that state. Drained it out completely and put in a fresh chemical mix.

Maintenance flagged the cleaner near bay 2 for a full changeout after quality started seeing failures on the last two batches. The bath was murky. Emptied it completely, cleaned the tank walls, and refilled with fresh solution.

Monthly check on the transducer faces was due today on the unit in cell 1. Found scale buildup on two of the elements in the lower array. Took the brush to them and logged the condition in the maintenance book.
Start of month inspection on the line 5 cleaner — the transducer array had pitting on one face, maybe 1.5 mm deep. Not over the replacement limit but flagged it for monitoring next cycle.

During a scheduled downtime window someone noticed caked-on residue on the transducer surfaces in the unit near the parts wash entry — wasn't the monthly check date yet but we cleaned them off while we had the machine down anyway.

Quarterly check on the immersion heater in unit 2 was on the schedule today. Resistance came back at 24 ohms — outside the normal band. Flagged it for replacement before it starts causing warm-up problems.

The cleaner in the back corner took almost 40 minutes to reach operating temperature this morning, way longer than the usual 10 to 15. Did a resistance check on the element and the reading was off. Needs a replacement.
The pressure gauge on the filter housing hit 17 psi this morning — normally sits around 8 to 10. Time to swap the cartridge before it starts bypassing dirty fluid back into the tank.

The filtration unit on line 3 was showing elevated restriction — pressure differential indicator was in the red zone. Maintenance swapped the filter element during the lunch break and flow came back up immediately.
Just finished replacing the generator on unit 1 and ran a post-install calibration with the hydrophone. Acoustic power output was 8% below reference — had to adjust before putting it back in service.

Quarterly calibration was due on the cleaner at the east end of the shop. Frequency was within band but the acoustic power reading came out 6% under spec. Logged it and notified the tech for adjustment.

Needed to pull the transducer array for replacement on the unit in cell 4. Had to lock out the whole machine first — hit estop on the panel, threw the main disconnect, and put the lock on before anyone went near the tank.

Scheduled drain and internal inspection on unit 3 this afternoon. Did the full isolation at the start of the window — main power cut and tagged before any crew went in. Standard practice before anyone climbs in that tank.

A fitting came loose during fill on the unit at station 7 and dumped maybe two liters of cleaner on the floor outside the berm. Floor sensor alarmed. Got the spill kit out of the cabinet right away and notified safety.

Second shift reported fluid in the aisle near the cleaner at station 7 — not inside the pan, out where people walk. Smelled like the cleaning chemical. Paused the machine and cleaned it up before anyone slipped on it.

A technician's sleeve got too close to the loading mechanism while the cleaner was cycling. Someone hit the nearest red button immediately. Machine stopped dead. We cleared the area and waited for the supervisor before touching anything.

Saw smoke coming from behind the control cabinet on the line 1 cleaner. Didn't wait to figure out the cause — hit estop and backed everyone off. Turned out to be a smoldering cable tie but we verified the panel was dead before we went back in.

Start of first shift Monday, the line 4 cleaner was completely cold and off from the weekend. Went through the whole power-on sequence — got the bath heating, waited for it to come up to temp, then brought the ultrasonics online. Had parts running by 6:50 AM.
Monday morning, brought all three cleaners online from fully off. The unit near the dock took a bit longer to warm up than the others but all three were at running temp and ultrasonics on by 6:45 AM.

End of second shift, took the cleaner down the normal way — turned off the transducers first, then the heater, let the bath cool a few minutes, then killed main power and pulled the disconnect. Ready for the night crew or maintenance.

Planned maintenance window tonight so we shut the cleaner on line 2 down early. Ran the full power-down sequence in order and isolated the main breaker before the maintenance crew showed up so they could go straight to work.

After the cleaning run on line 3 this morning, ran the UV lamp over the batch before sending them to assembly. Found three parts with contamination showing up clearly under the light. Pulled them and sent them to the rework stand.

End of the morning run, did the standard part check with the UV lamp. Most of the batch looked fine but one part had a film on it that lit up under the light. Sent it back for another cycle rather than let it go to assembly.

Post-clean check on the batch from cell 5 — UV scan showed residue on about 10% of the parts, which is way above the usual rejection rate. Logged all the failures and moved the rejected tray to the rework station. Going to check the bath condition next.

Start-of-shift check on the cleaner at station 2 — pulled a sample and ran it through the refractometer. Reading came back at 4.5%, which is under where we want it. Flagged it for the tech to adjust the concentration before running production.

Quality alert came through about inconsistent cleaning results on the last batch. Pulled a sample from the unit on line 6 and checked it — refractometer said 9.2%, over the top of the acceptable range. Bath is too strong, needs dilution.

Routine morning check on the fluid strength in the corner cleaner. Reading came back at 6.1% which is right in the middle of the range. Second shift hadn't logged their check so we recorded it for both and left a note.

Line 3 spindle drive went dark on us right around 6 AM. Motor just kicked out and the whole line stopped. I could see the current climbing on the display before it dropped—was pulling way too many amps and then the unit tripped itself.

The drive cabinet near the loading dock started pulling way more amps than normal right before it shut down. I watched the number on the HMI climb past the red line and then boom—motor stopped, line down. Current spike before the trip was obvious.

Drive on the conveyor line threw a fit when the motor was decelerating too fast coming off a high-speed run. Bus voltage climbed way past where it should sit and the unit shut itself down. Reading on the display showed it well over the ceiling.

Right after maintenance swapped the motor on cell 7, the drive faulted out on the very first startup attempt. Bus voltage reading was sitting way above the upper limit before the drive even got to speed. Looked like the regen braking config was wrong for the new motor.

Line 2 saw the drive drop out unexpectedly during a normal decel cycle. The bus voltage number climbed past safe limits and the unit tripped before anyone could react. Whole thing was over in a couple seconds.

The drive in bay 4 has been throwing a low-voltage warning on and off all morning but it is still running. The bus reading on the display is sitting lower than we normally see it—looks like it drifted down slowly since the last shift check, not a sudden drop.

Third shift noticed the bus reading on line 5's main drive creeping down through the night. Was not a sudden thing at all—just slowly fell below where it should be over two or three hours. Drive is still running but the value has not recovered on its own.

Everything went dead at once on bay 6—no ramp down, no warning, just an instant blackout on the drive. The bus reading dropped to basically nothing in a split second. Scared the hell out of us. Nothing gradual about it at all.

Second shift, the drive by compressor row just collapsed completely. One second it was running fine, next second zero volts on the bus. Did not even alarm before it dropped—just instant total loss. Nothing like the slow undervoltage issue we had on line 5 last week.

The amber light on the drive cabinet in cell 3 came on around 2 PM. Unit is still running and has not shut down, but the temperature reading is definitely higher than normal. Happened on a real hot afternoon—fan seems to be spinning okay, nothing tripped.

Operator on bay 8 called me over because the drive cabinet felt hotter than usual and had a blinking amber light. Still operational, fan appeared to be running, but the temperature display is sitting in the yellow zone. Has not shut itself down.

Drive on line 1 cooked itself and shut down hard mid-production. By the time I got there the heat sink was way too hot to touch and everything was offline. Unit had tripped itself completely—motor not moving, drive totally dead.

The big drive in the stamping area went down hard during second shift—thermal protection kicked in and killed it completely. When maintenance got there the temperature reading was past the red mark and the drive was stone cold stopped. Not a warning this time, a full shutdown.

The GFI tripped on the drive cabinet near dock 3. Electrician says it looks like an insulation problem somewhere in the wiring to the motor. Circuit is dead, fault light is lit solid, and we are keeping everyone away until the root cause is found.

The drive on line 6 is making an unusual low hum from the cooling section—sounds like the fan is laboring a bit. It is still spinning and the drive is still running, but the fan does not sound right and there is a yellow indicator lit on the panel. Heatsink is running warmer than normal.

Second shift noticed the cabinet on press 9 was running hotter than usual. Fan seems to be turning but it is noticeably slower than it should be—you can hear the difference just standing next to it. Drive has not shut down, still producing parts.

Line 3 drive went into emergency shutdown around 10 AM. I checked the back of the cabinet and the cooling fan is completely dead—no movement, totally silent back there. Nothing like the sluggish fan issue on press 9; this one is not turning at all.

PM schedule showed the filter on the bay 5 drive cabinet was due for swap last Thursday. We were running behind on preventive work but maintenance finally flagged it today. No faults, no alarms, the unit is running fine—just hit the calendar interval.

Line 7 drive cabinet filter came up on the weekly PM checklist during the morning walkdown. Filter is not dirty enough to be causing any issues and the airflow looks okay, but the calendar says it is time so we are swapping it out on schedule.

Drive cabinet on press line 2 started running warm and the pressure indicator behind the filter was reading high. Pulled the filter and it was packed solid with metal dust—nowhere near the normal swap schedule but it clearly needs changing now.

The airflow out of the drive cabinet near welding station 4 dropped off noticeably during first shift. Maintenance tech checked the differential pressure gauge and the reading was way off the charts—filter was completely blocked with grinding debris from the nearby operation.

The six-month capacitor check came due on the main drive cabinet in bay 3. No issues noted in the machine, nothing unusual on the floor—just the time to do the scheduled visual and measurement inspection per the PM calendar.

Annual connection check came due on the line 5 drive cabinet this week. No symptoms, no faults, running fine—just the scheduled torque verification per the preventive maintenance plan. Maintenance has the wrench out.

The interior of the drive cabinet in bay 6 looks like a dust bunny farm. Have not done a thorough clean-out since the last quarterly PM and it is getting thick in there. Need to blow it out before the buildup becomes a real problem.

PM audit on line 4 flagged the drive cabinet interior as overdue for cleaning. A lot of fine metal dust from the nearby grinding operation has been working its way inside and coating everything. Maintenance wants it cleaned before the next quarterly review.

Thermal camera pass on the drive in cell 8 showed certain sections of the heat sink running hotter than the rest. Fins look plugged up on one side with compacted debris—drive is okay for now but needs a compressed air treatment to get airflow back through the fins.

Line 2 motor has been running slightly slow for the past week—production noticed parts are taking a hair longer than they should through the cycle. We need to verify the drive output actually matches what we commanded before assuming it is a mechanical issue.

Electrician needs to swap a burned contactor inside the cabinet on press 6. Nothing is wrong with the drive itself—we just need power dead and tagged before he opens that door and starts touching things inside.
PM team is doing the annual terminal inspection on line 3's drive cabinet. Standard pre-work before anyone goes inside—disconnect and personal lock on before the cabinet door opens, same as always.

There was a burning smell coming from the direction of the main VFD cabinet on line 1 and someone reported seeing a wisp of smoke curling out of the top vents. We hit the red mushroom button and called the supervisor without waiting.

Electrician locked out the drive cabinet on bay 7 but wanted to confirm the bus was actually dead before reaching in to swap the IGBT module. Called me over to verify the voltage reading on the internal bus sensor before he touched anything near the capacitors.

After we shut down and locked out the line 5 drive for a contactor swap, the tech would not open the main bus covers until someone confirmed there was no stored charge on the bus. Standard safety check before the work started—those caps can hold a lot of juice even after shutdown.

First shift coming on and line 4 drive cabinet needs to come up from a cold weekend shutdown. Everything is off, no faults, just running through the normal checks before we start pulling product for the morning run.

End of second shift and we need to bring the line 6 drive down properly before the maintenance crew comes in for the overnight window. Nothing wrong with the unit—just taking it down clean at end of shift.
Production manager called it for an early shutdown on line 3 due to low orders on the afternoon of the 12th. Need to take the drive down in the correct order before the crew leaves for the day.

Electrician found a loose lug that caused the overcurrent trip on press 5's drive earlier this morning. He fixed the connection, confirmed nothing else is damaged, and cleared the fault display. Now we need to bring the drive back up and confirm it runs right before we call the line good.

Line 3 feeder stopped dead this morning about 20 minutes into first shift. Nothing coming through the exit chute. Got a look through the side window and there was a bracket wedged sideways across the spiral track about a third of the way up — totally blocking everything behind it.

Feeder on line 4 keeps going in and out all shift — runs fine for maybe ten seconds, goes quiet for five, then kicks back up. Hopper looks half full, so it's not running out. Like it's choking on and off.

The unit at press 7 is acting real inconsistent today. Parts coming in these sudden bursts then nothing for a few seconds. Watched the funnel area at the top and it looks like stuff is clumping together at that entry point — sticking and releasing.

Intermittent stoppages on the feeder at cell 2. Bowl sounds like it's running the whole time but the chute output is choppy. No fault light, no empty alarm. Think the parts are blocking each other at the top and then breaking loose in batches.

Rate counter at station 5 has been sitting in the red zone for a couple minutes but the machine is still humming. Parts are trickling through the chute — maybe a third of what we normally see. Has been like this since the last break.

Bowl at line 2 is humming but absolutely nothing coming down the chute. Zero. One second it was running normal, next second the output just died — no parts at all. Thing is still vibrating, lights are on, but the exit channel is bone dry.

Output display on the line 6 feeder just shows nothing. Like it flipped off in an instant — not a gradual slowdown. Machine sounds totally alive but the PPM readout is at zero and the downstream robot is waiting on parts.

Parts flooding out the exit on line 6 too fast. The rotary table downstream is getting buried and parts are piling up past the stops. Count display is way above our upper spec — never seen it that high.
The slide under the feeder near the robot arm at bay 3 is overflowing. Parts spilling off the end of the track. Throughput is way beyond normal — thing is running way hotter than setpoint.

Red fault light on the control box by the line 3 feeder came on and the whole machine went dark — just cut out. Panel display is showing a fault code, not a normal stop. There's a faint warm smell near the bottom of the enclosure.

Feeder on the right side of bay 2 sounds anemic — bowl is barely moving, like it's running at maybe 20 percent. Parts are barely creeping up the spiral. Ran totally fine yesterday afternoon so something changed overnight.

Third shift reported the feeder seemed sluggish when they started up, kept running anyway. Morning crew came in and the bowl is just barely oscillating — you can see it moving but it's weak. No trip, no fault code, just underpowered.

Feeder at press 12 is moving parts but at about half the usual amplitude. Bowl barely shakes. No alarms tripped, but the vibration is clearly weaker than it should be — like the drive isn't getting what it needs.

Yellow caution light came on at the feeder panel by dock 3. Bowl is still running fine and parts are still coming through — no slowdown yet. Light's been on for a few minutes now. Probably needs a reload soon.

Operator flagged me over to look at the amber indicator on the feeder at line 7 — it's flashing but the machine is still moving parts normally. No slowdown, no stop, just that warning lamp on the panel.

Panel light at the feeder near press 4 went amber about ten minutes into second shift. Production is still going, output still looks normal. Just a heads-up that supply is getting low — not urgent yet but needs attention.
Nothing coming out of the line 5 feeder at all — completely stopped. Looked inside the top and there is nothing left. Bottom of the bowl is fully visible, bone dry. Line went idle waiting on parts.
Robot at the loading station is reaching into empty air — no parts coming from the feeder. Peeked in the hopper and literally nothing left in there. Not a jam, not a fault — completely out of parts.

Reject chute at feeder 2 is getting hammered — parts keep looping back in bulk into the bowl. Way more rejects than normal, maybe one in five or six. The vision system indicator keeps flashing. Something is definitely wrong with how parts are being oriented.

Feeder by the stamping press is rattling more than usual — not terrible, but definitely louder and coarser than the normal tone. It's been going like this for the last 20 minutes of the shift. Machine is still running and putting out parts, just noisier.

Something sounds different about the feeder on line 1 — has this extra buzz or low rattle underneath the normal hum. Been there all shift. Parts are still flowing fine, no fault lights showing, just sounds off compared to yesterday.

Loud bang from the feeder at station 4 — thing started shaking so hard the whole stand was moving back and forth. We backed away from it immediately. Never heard it that violent before. Took it down right away.

Feeder near the loading dock started vibrating violently and you could see the bowl bouncing on its mount. The noise was metallic and harsh, like something loose thrashing inside. Everyone cleared the area and someone hit the stop.

Parts on the bowl track at press 9 are not sliding cleanly — there's an oily film or fine dust build-up on the spiral surface. Parts are dragging instead of gliding. PM sticker on the side says this one is overdue for a wipe-down.
PM calendar shows the spring contact lube is due on the feeder at cell 3. Last service entry in the log was about six weeks back. No symptoms, just scheduled.
Maintenance order came through for the feeder by line 2 — spring mounting surfaces are at their lubrication interval per the PM schedule. Flagging this for the next planned downtime window.

Did a maintenance walk-down and one of those flat metal strips at the base of the bowl feeder on line 6 looks slightly bent. Hard to say if it's damage or just dirty, but it needs a proper look before we assume it's fine.

Coating inside the bowl at feeder 7 is flaking near the outer edge. Found a small piece of liner material sitting in the output tray when we checked the quality pull. That's a contamination issue — have to address it now.

Quality walk flagged the bowl on line 3 feeder — there is a crack in the interior surface coating about four inches long. Parts passing over it could be picking up debris. Can't let it keep running like that.
Operator says the gauge on feeder 4 is reading half-full but he put in two completely full bins this morning. It should be showing near-full. Reading and reality are way off.

Quarterly calibration check is due on the bowl level sensor at line 8. Also had a complaint last week that the low-level warning came on way too early — bowl was still plenty full when the alarm triggered.
Need to get inside the feeder housing at station 2 to reposition the track guide. Nobody touches the inside of that machine until we do the full isolation — too much moving hardware in there.

Maintenance crew is swapping the bowl liner on line 5 feeder. Before anyone starts unbolting anything, power has to be fully cut and locked. Checking the work order — it says full energy isolation required before entry.
Electrician needs hands-on access to the coil assembly on the feeder at press 7. Going to be inside the unit, not just panel work. Full energy isolation has to happen before he goes in.
Someone knocked a parts bin near feeder 3 and small brackets scattered everywhere — whole aisle section is covered. Real slip hazard for anyone walking through that area.

Overflow from the feeder chute on line 4 dumped parts onto the floor behind the robot cell during the run. Roughly a square meter of small hardware sitting on concrete. Nobody hurt but it needs to be dealt with before the next pass.

Somebody hit the red button near feeder 6 and everything is locked out. Panel shows E-stop active. Don't know yet if it was automatic or a person, but it needs to be checked and cleared before we can restart.

E-stop on the line 1 feeder went active — machine is completely dead. Could be a manual hit, could be the system did it on its own. Either way we have to figure out what caused it and get through the reset process before the line can come back up.

Coming in for first shift and the feeder at station 3 is sitting cold and dark — needs to be brought up before the line starts. Display shows no faults from yesterday. Just needs to go through the normal startup.
Tech just signed off on the work order for feeder at bay 4 — maintenance window is done and everything is reassembled. Need to get it running again through the checklist before production resumes.
Shift is wrapping up and the feeder at line 2 needs to be brought down clean before we leave for the night. Production quota is done, machine has been running solid all day.
End of day on line 7 feeder — need to power it down properly before the weekend maintenance window kicks off tonight. No issues all shift, just a routine end-of-production shutdown.

Screen went blank on camera 3 right after startup, no picture at all. Line 3 was sitting dead for about 10 minutes before anyone noticed parts were running through unchecked. Had to call it out over the radio. — D. Kowalski, 2nd shift

After the lunch break the whole right-side display on the unit by the loading dock came back with nothing on it. Kept blinking, no image at all. Someone had to run product blind until the vision tech got there. — J. Park, 3rd shift

Lights inside the inspection zone looked washed out and kind of yellowish, noticeably dimmer than normal. It was fine at 6 AM but by noon you could barely see the part surface on the monitor. Crept up on us slow. — R. Singh, 1st shift

The system kept throwing up a yellow banner — not the red alarm, just a yellow advisory — and the ring lights were obviously less bright than last week. Took most of the morning to get bad enough to notice. Definitely not sudden. — C. Barba, 2nd shift

Lights just cut out. One second they were full brightness over the nest, the next second pitch black. No dimming beforehand, just gone. Had to shout to get everybody to stop the line immediately. — A. Duda, 2nd shift

The arm that kicks the bad ones into the reject chute just wouldn't budge. You could hear it trying — thumping — but nothing moved. Parts were piling up past the gate and going into the good bin. — B. Koonce, 3rd shift

Reject chute door was stuck completely solid. Heard one hard thump then nothing. Tried to push it by hand and there was something wedged in the mechanism — wouldn't shift at all. — L. Martinez, 1st shift
The divert flap froze up in the middle of a cycle. The controller HMI showed it as active but you could see with your own eyes it wasn't going anywhere. Completely immobilized. — S. Patel, 2nd shift

Gate's moving but it's lazy about it. Takes a beat too long after the reject signal and some of the flagged parts are already past it by the time the flap swings over. Nothing stuck, just slow. — M. Chen, 1st shift

Quality pulled 30 parts out of the red bin at the end of the shift and 28 of them checked out perfectly good. Vision system's being way too jumpy on the surface check. Good parts going in the scrap pile. — D. Stein, 1st shift

Reject count was almost 1 in 5 today on line 2. Ran a bunch of them by hand inspection and they all pass visual and dimensional. The vision box is seeing things that aren't there. — T. Adeyemi, 3rd shift

Found a cracked housing in a finished shipping box that should have been pulled at the camera check. That part definitely went through — it had the PASS label on it. Something's not triggering on the bad ones. — K. Brown, QA

Customer called in a complaint. Scratched parts showed up in their incoming inspection, and our system had them stamped PASS and shipped. Defects are getting through the camera station without being flagged. — R. Cho, quality coordinator

A yellow alarm came up on the vision controller box — something about camera temperature. System was still fully running, nothing tripped or stopped. Just that amber warning sitting there. — F. DiMaggio, 2nd shift

Got a blinking amber on the panel at the inspection station on the north side. Nothing stopped, cameras were still live and producing images. Tech said it was running warm but hadn't hit the critical cutoff yet. — B. Otieno, 1st shift

System threw a focus error but the part design hasn't changed. Looking at the monitor you can see a smear over the center of the image — looks like oil mist or something on the glass in front of the lens. — A. Rossi, 1st shift

Camera 2 on the unit by the south wall has been showing a milky haze for a couple hours. Parts look blurry on-screen. Same thing happened last month after the press next door had a coolant overspray incident. — H. Kim, 2nd shift

Light over inspection zone 2 looks uneven — super bright right in the center and noticeably dark around the edges. Been like that for a few shifts, not totally out, just a patchy spread. — O. Bell, 1st shift
Every part that sits in the nest looks like it has a shadow on one side in the camera image. Ring light isn't spreading evenly anymore. Pretty sure the diffuser is worn out. — G. Cruz, 3rd shift
Reject arm is making a grinding squeak on every single cycle. Moves fine, no hesitation, but the noise is getting louder each shift. Been building all week. — P. Hadley, 2nd shift
Gate is squealing on every stroke out here on line 4. Maintenance walked by and said it's overdue for grease — nothing mechanically broken but it sounds like metal on metal. — N. Watts, 1st shift

PM calendar says calibration was due last Tuesday. Nobody got to it during that shift and it's been sitting past the window ever since. Still running product through but we're overdue. — J. Ferris, process tech

Controller had a banner on it when I powered up this morning that said something like CALIBRATION DUE. Been about a month since the last one, or maybe longer. Just sitting there on the screen at startup. — W. Osei, 1st shift
Monthly PM checklist came back and it flagged the calibration as overdue by 6 days. Nothing crashed or alarmed hard but the tracking sheet shows we blew past the interval. — C. Lin, maintenance

Parts are consistently poking out to the left side of the camera frame on camera 2. Looks like the view has drifted since sometime last week. Not throwing an alarm yet but something's visibly off-center. — T. Russo, 1st shift

Controller inside the enclosure on the east line tripped a high-temp advisory. Stuck my hand near the intake vent and airflow is barely there — feels completely restricted compared to normal. — B. Huang, maintenance

There's a hissing sound coming from right around the reject arm cylinder. Air is bleeding out somewhere on the actuator block. Gate still cycles but pressure feels low and it's definitely slower than it should be. — R. Petrov, 2nd shift

Need to go inside the enclosure to swap out a camera mount bracket. Walked up and the conveyor was still enabled and no lock was on the disconnect. Nobody had isolated it before starting. — P. Amara, maintenance

Tech had their hand right next to the camera bracket for a lens swap and the station hadn't been properly de-energized before they went in. Shift supervisor caught it and stopped them immediately. — Y. Tanaka, area supervisor

Knocked over a small bottle of lens cleaner while prepping for the PM — it went right off the shelf and splashed onto the conveyor belt below the camera mount. Might have gotten into the belt drive area. — C. Santos, 1st shift
Part went sideways on the belt and was about to get dragged up into the camera frame mount at high speed. Hit the red mushroom without thinking. Whole line stopped instantly. — L. Thomas, 1st shift

Came in at 6 AM for day shift and the station was completely dark — nobody from nights had powered it up before they left. Had to walk through the whole boot process before we could start running parts. — D. Kowalski, 1st shift

End of 2nd shift and the cameras were still live, system running, when 3rd shift showed up. Nobody had gone through the power-down steps before leaving. Third shift didn't know what state anything was in. — T. Cruz, 2nd shift

Station was left fully on over the weekend. Came in Monday and the controller had been running with no product for two days straight. Trying to get better about the end-of-week power-off routine. — S. Williams, maintenance

Switched over to the new bracket part number after the morning break but the vision box was still on the old housing recipe. First dozen-plus pieces ran through on the wrong inspection program before anyone caught it. — M. Baxter, 1st shift

Start-of-shift check this morning — ran the known-bad part with the surface scratch through and it came back with a green PASS. That's supposed to be an automatic reject. Something's wrong with how it's reading right now. — R. Andersen, 1st shift

Post-PM check using the reference samples. The sample with the subsurface void that's supposed to always trigger a reject came through clean with no alarm. Couldn't release the line until we figured out what changed. — F. Nakamura, process engineer

Line 3 coolant supply was running sluggish this morning around 6am. The gauge at the pump skid near the south wall was hanging around 38 PSI the whole time — nowhere near where it should be. Pump was still spinning, just not pushing enough. Called it in at start of first shift.

Came in for night shift handoff and the day guys said the unit up by the stamping cells had been weak all afternoon. Checked the digital readout — 43 PSI and holding there steady. Motor running fine, nothing tripped. Just not enough push in the system, gradual the whole time.

All hell broke loose on line 2 around 2pm. One second we had normal pressure, next second the needle dropped to the floor — like 8 PSI in less than 5 seconds. Water started backing up at the machining cells. I've never seen it go that fast. This wasn't a slow thing at all.

Third shift, the pump by the west dock just cratered. No warning, just a huge instantaneous drop on the display. Went from about 62 PSI down to basically nothing before I even got to the panel. Heard something give way somewhere in the line right after the pump tripped.

Middle of morning startup, the system pressure wiped out in under 5 seconds — I was watching the screen and it just fell off a cliff. Night crew said everything was fine at handoff an hour earlier. Totally different from the times we've seen it drift low over a shift.

The panel near the assembly cells was showing 91 PSI this morning — way past where we run. The relief valve didn't pop. I wasn't sure if something was stuck or if the setpoint got bumped. Pressure just kept climbing above the ceiling before I caught it.

After we brought the pump back online after lunch, discharge was reading over 88 PSI. I could hear the pipes creaking a bit. Nothing burst, but the numbers were clearly above the max the supervisor posted on the board. First shift, unit near shipping.

The parts washer on the east end wasn't getting enough water throughput during first shift. Pump sounded like it was working, but flow at the tool was way down — slower than I've ever seen it running. The pump wasn't dead, just starved. Pressure gauge looked roughly okay.

Maintenance log from last night: line 4 water supply was trickling during the second half of third shift. Motor humming away, no faults on the board, but the flow meter at the control station was reading about 9 GPM. About half of normal throughput, pump still running.

Pump on the main skid was screaming — running full tilt, sounded angry — but absolutely zero water moving anywhere on line 1. The machining cells went dry completely. Motor pulling amps, nothing coming out the other end. Something is totally blocked or the impeller let go.

End of first shift, line 2 coolant stopped moving entirely but nobody had pressed the stop button. You could hear the motor still running. Flow indicator at the panel by the east wall showing a big fat zero. Not a pressure problem — dead stop on the water with the motor still going.

Did the weekly walkaround and the bladder tank near the pump room door was reading about 22 PSI on the pre-charge port. System pressure looked okay on the main gauge, but that accumulator isn't holding enough charge. It's been short-cycling more than normal too.

Noticed during the morning rounds that the expansion tank by the boiler room side keeps making the pump kick on and off too often — cycling maybe every 20 seconds. Checked the air charge gauge on the tank body itself — only showing 25 PSI. Whole thing feels waterlogged.

Motor housing on pump unit 1 near the loading dock was too hot to even get close to — could feel the heat from two feet away. The thermal alarm light on the panel was flashing red. We'd been running it hard all day on a rush order and it just cooked itself.

Second shift complained about a burning smell near the pump skid on the south end. Checked the winding temp readout on the panel — showing 162 degrees Celsius. Fan blade on the motor might be broken or the vent slots are clogged with debris. It was definitely too hot.

MCC cabinet on the east wall threw a fault right at startup this morning. The indicator was solid red. The pump just wouldn't come on. Electrician on call said it looked like an overcurrent trip. Couldn't get anywhere with the normal start sequence from the operator panel.

During third shift the main pump tripped hard — nothing mechanical was wrong that I could see, but the drive cabinet next to the pump room door was showing a fault light. Couldn't restart from the operator panel at all. Had to call the E-tech out at 3am to sort it.

Phase loss fault at the motor control box near the compressor room — happened twice on second shift. First reset it came back, second time it stayed tripped. Fuses looked okay visually but something is flaky in the circuit. Not a mechanical issue, all electrical.

Walkaround this morning and there's a slow drip coming from around the shaft area on unit 1 near the east dock. Like one drop every few seconds, leaving a small wet spot on the floor plate. Pump running fine otherwise, good pressure and flow — not gushing, just weeping at the back.

First shift operator noted a damp ring forming under the pump by the filter housing. You can see where it's been seeping for a while — there's a mineral stain building on the base plate. Still very minor, no spray, no puddle forming — just a slow seep right at the shaft packing area.

Water was spraying like a sprinkler head from a fitting near the ceiling on the pump station north wall. Hit the ceiling tiles, soaked two operators who were nearby. The whole area was getting drenched within seconds. Nobody had stopped anything yet when I got there — pumps still running.

500-hour PM came due on the main pump this week. Maintenance coordinator wanted the seal check done before second shift started. Pump had been running smooth so nobody expected surprises, but still needed to do the shaft inspection and sign off the condition in the logbook.

Planned inspection on the pump unit near the assembly area — just the regular look at the shaft seals as part of the PM schedule. Nothing obviously wrong but we were due at 500 hours, so the tech went through the inspection routine to document current condition and check for early wear.

Differential pressure across the inlet strainer on the main unit was riding at 6 PSI all morning — been creeping up for a couple days. That basket is definitely plugged up. Water wasn't getting through clean enough. Needed a swap before the restriction got bad enough to starve the pump.

The screen basket on the suction side was caked with debris when maintenance pulled it — iron filings and some rubber bits from upstream machining. The delta-P gauge on that strainer section was pegged above the change-out number. Definitely time to drop in a fresh element.

250-hour grease interval came up on both pump units this morning per the PM board. One of the techs mentioned the bearing housings felt slightly rough underfoot when walking the floor last week. No failure, just time for the scheduled greasing on both units before it becomes a problem.

Both pumps on the north end were due for bearing service. The PM tag on unit 2 was actually overdue by about 30 hours — someone missed it last cycle. Housings felt warm during rounds but no abnormal noise yet. Just needed the grease service completed to get back on schedule.

Quarterly PRV test was on the schedule for this week. Last time it was checked was three months back by day shift and it passed fine then. No complaints about it lately, just doing the required functional check to confirm it will still open at the right point if we ever need it.

Engineering asked for the safety valve on the discharge header to be tested after the system ran at elevated pressure last week. Needed to verify it would open at the correct setpoint and reseat cleanly afterward. Strictly a verify-and-document exercise, not a repair or adjustment job.

After the inspection confirmed the accumulator was undercharged, maintenance brought out the nitrogen bottle to top it off. Tank was confirmed isolated from the system first. Pre-charge was brought back up to spec and the short-cycling stopped right after the fill was done.

The expansion tank by the east pump room needed the air charge restored — it had bled down since last quarter. The tech connected the nitrogen rig to the Schrader valve on the tank while it was off the line. After the fill, checked the gauge and the system stopped hunting immediately.

Weekly vibe readings were due on the pump skids this Monday. One tech mentioned unit 2 felt a tiny bit rougher underfoot when walking by it last Thursday. Nothing alarming, just doing the scheduled measurement to see if the numbers confirm anything before it gets worse.

Maintenance was going in to replace the mechanical seal on unit 1 and needed the whole pump station made safe first. Electrician and plumber both had to be involved. All stored energy had to be killed and physically locked before anyone was allowed to open that pump casing.

A plumber needed access to the main discharge header to install a new tap for a branch line. Before he could cut into the live pipe, the pump had to be de-energized and the water isolated completely. Standard isolation before anyone puts a torch or a saw to that piping.

Found a puddle on the pump room floor this morning — maybe 3 square feet of standing water. Couldn't see any active drip anywhere obvious on the pipes or fittings. No spraying, no gushing, no seal weeping visible. Just water on the floor with no obvious live source still running.

A contractor working near the pump skid slipped and went down hard. Supervisor called for an immediate halt to all equipment in the area before anyone else moved in to help. Everything needed to stop right now — no time to go through any kind of normal sequence.

Saw sparks coming from the junction box mounted next to the pump motor during third shift. Didn't know if it was a real electrical fault or a fluke, but the area had to be cleared and the equipment killed instantly. No time for a normal wind-down — just needed it stopped.

First shift bring-up after the weekend idle — nothing wrong, just the standard sequence to get the water system running before the machining lines started at 6am. Needed to verify flow and pressure were both good before telling the production supervisor the lines were ready.

End of day Friday, production done for the week. Supervisor called for water service to be wound down before the plant went into weekend mode. Nothing broken, nothing alarming — just the routine close-out on the pump station at the end of a normal production week.

A maintenance window was scheduled for Saturday morning, so the pump system had to be brought down in a controlled way during Friday night third shift. No faults, no alarms going into it — just getting everything parked properly before the crew came in to do their repair work.

Quality came around during first shift for the daily water sampling — someone upstream had changed a coolant concentrate mix and they wanted to make sure nothing cloudy was getting into the process water circuit. Standard daily sample collection at the tap near the pump room door.

The inline turbidity monitor on the main supply line was showing a slightly elevated reading after startup this morning — looked a bit murky on the display. Quality tech wanted a grab sample and a sensor confirmation before releasing the line to production. Daily check but with a bit more urgency than usual.

Line 3 second shift, the wave machine HMI started showing amber on the pot temp readout around 2 AM. Wasn't dramatically low, just hovering around 242 when it should be sitting at 250. Boards were still running fine but I flagged it before we got any cold joint complaints. Temp had been drifting down slowly for maybe 30 minutes.

Machine by the east loading dock crept about six degrees cold this morning. Noticed the temp display just dipping under the green band but nothing alarming — no alarm horn, just the indicator light going yellow. First shift lead called me over. Pot was still running, just gradually losing heat.

Tech on line 7. Pot temp reading 241 at start of the second run cycle. Heat wasn't keeping up — gradual drift, definitely not a sudden thing. Sent a board to QC as a precaution and kept an eye on the trend. No panic, just a slow walk down.

Middle of third shift on the south wave unit, pot temp dropped like a rock — went from 260 down to 232 in under three minutes. Never seen it fall that fast. Something failed in the heating system. Hit the stop immediately and called it in.

Something went wrong with the heater on line 2. Temp was fine at the 6 AM check then an alarm screamed and the readout was plummeting. Must have lost a heating element — this wasn't a drift, it was in freefall. Called maintenance right away.

Second shift, unit 4 by the loading dock. Operator reported the pot temp nosedived — said it lost almost 20 degrees before anyone reacted. Not a slow creep, a genuine collapse. Machine was shut down on the spot. Heater fault suspected.

Line 5 threw an overtemp alarm mid-morning — display was showing 284, well above where we run. Red light on the panel, alarm beeping steady. Pulled the board batch and held production. Trim must have walked up on its own.
Flux tank indicator on line 3 dropped into the red band around noon. Wasn't empty but the low-level light came on and production would have been at risk by end of shift if nobody refilled it.

Flux reservoir on the unit near dock 4 ran lower than we like to see it — around the 15 percent mark on the sight glass. Machine was still running but we were close to losing prime on the pump. Called for a refill.

Maintenance call on line 6. Flux pressure gauge spiked past the rated mark on the dial. Pump was making a different noise than normal and the needle was buried in the red. Shut the pump down before anything could blow.

Night shift on the south wing wave unit — flux line pressure went to high alarm. Not a gradual rise, jumped up pretty quick. Worried about the spray nozzle taking damage. Stopped the pump and called maintenance.

Line 3 conveyor was dragging this morning — boards moving noticeably slower than normal through the machine. Board transit timer was coming in long on every cycle. No jam, no fault light, just sluggish movement.

First shift noticed boards on line 7 taking longer to transit the machine than the recipe calls for. Speed display on the panel was reading below the setpoint. No stoppage, drive was still turning, just slower than programmed.

Complete halt on the conveyor during second shift on line 4. Board stuck dead in the middle of the machine. Drive motor was humming and energized but absolutely nothing was moving. Had to call maintenance to get in there.
Line 2 north unit, board went in and never came out the other side. Waited a full minute, nothing. Conveyor was frozen solid with product inside. Not slow — totally stopped. Chain was locked up.

Third shift, unit by dock 2. PCB got wedged somehow and brought the whole conveyor to a complete standstill. Motor was still energized but the chain wasn't moving at all. Different from when it just slows down — this was a full stop with product inside.
QC flagged a batch from line 3 — pads on the back side of the board barely wetted. Went and looked through the inspection window and the wave looked really flat. Wasn't reaching the boards properly.

Line 7 second shift. Operator said the solder window looked thin — wave wasn't cresting like normal. A few reference boards came out with insufficient fillets on the heavier component leads. Wave running low.
Got solder bridges all over the connector on boards coming off line 3. Looked in the wave window and the wave was surging way up, practically splashing around the nozzle lip. Batch pulled for rework.

Second shift, line 2. Solder was visibly overflowing the nozzle area during every board pass. Boards had solder balls and bridging everywhere when they came out the exit side. Wave clearly running way higher than spec.

Line 4 preheat zone showed a cold reading this morning — well under what it should be for our current board spec. Flux wasn't fully activating; you could still smell the carrier solvent at the solder zone entrance. No alarm horn going off though.

Critical alarm on line 5 — preheat blasted past 160 and was still climbing when I got there. Red alarm light on, horn going steady. Boards in the preheat zone were visibly discolored. Stopped everything immediately.

Middle of second shift on the east wing wave unit. Preheat thermocouple reading 168 degrees with the critical alarm horn screaming. Way outside spec — thin PCB substrate was starting to show warping at the preheat exit zone.

Motor fault on line 7 — the conveyor drive tripped out and a fault light came on the panel. Conveyor stopped but this was different from a jam — the VFD display was showing an overcurrent error code. No obvious mechanical blockage when I looked.

Line 3 second shift. Conveyor drive made a buzzing sound then the fault relay tripped and the drive locked out. Controller display showed an overcurrent fault. No jam found, nothing wedged in the chain. Electrical issue with the motor.

Noticed a small drip forming on the side of the pot near the front nozzle fitting on line 4. Tiny — just beading up and dripping slow. Machine was still running, nothing on the floor yet, completely contained to the fitting area.

Line 6 during maintenance check. Found a slow seep at one of the pot body gasket joints. Silver bead forming and dripping maybe once every few seconds. Not flowing freely, contained to the machine base. Someone needs to look at that gasket seal.

Emergency on line 5 — solder came out everywhere. Large pool forming on the machine base and starting to run onto the floor. Smoking and burning smell immediately. Hit the red button and got everyone back from the area.

Night shift, south wave unit. Catastrophic failure — solder was pouring out of the pot, heard a loud bang first. Floor around the machine was covered in a wide area. Nobody got hurt but it was bad. Full shutdown called.

Line 3 pot surface had a thick grey skin on it — way more than usual for this point in the shift. Dark crusty layer covering most of the surface. Needed skimming before it started getting pulled down into the wave pump.
Maintenance note on line 7: hit the four-hour interval and the pot surface looks rough. Grey layer covering a good chunk of the top. Scheduled dross skim is overdue by half a shift.
Flux pump on line 4 started sounding like it was working harder than usual. Checked the pressure gauges and the drop across the filter housing was reading high. Filter's clogged, needs swapping out.
Hit the eight-week service interval on the line 2 flux system. Pressure differential across the filter also looking elevated even before we're at flow. Time to change it out per the PM schedule.
Conveyor fingers on line 6 have got a real flux buildup — dark brown residue coating all the finger tips. Boards coming out with flux smear transfer on the edges. Due for a cleaning.
Wave profile on line 5 looking uneven through the inspection glass — one side of the nozzle seems partially blocked. Left side cresting higher than the right. Nozzle clean was overdue by two days.

Board coverage coming off the line 3 flux station was uneven — dry patches right in the center of every board. Spray nozzle hasn't been calibrated in a while. Flow rate might be off or oscillation pattern drifted.

Wave on line 4 started looking shallow at the edges and the low-level indicator light came on. Not an emergency yet but pot definitely needs ingots added before next shift or we'll lose wave formation.
Line 2 second shift. Solder level sensor tripped the low indicator on the control panel. Wave was starting to look thin at the sides during board pass. Needs topping up before we go further.

Maintenance work order issued for replacing the conveyor chain on line 5. Crew needs to go inside the guarded area. Machine has to be fully locked out before anyone touches it. LOTO procedure requested.
Line 3 scheduled PM this weekend — both an electrician and a mechanical tech need inside the machine at the same time. All energy sources need isolated and documented before work starts.

Smoke alarm went off above line 6 wave unit during second shift. Didn't see open flames but there was smoke coming from the preheat area. Hit the e-stop and got everyone back from the machine immediately.

Third shift, line 2. Operator smelled burning and saw a small flash near the solder pot — looked like flux ignition. Triggered the emergency stop right away. Called for the fire extinguisher from the safety station.
